7 questions that feature \n\t\t\t\t\t15787 text conditional logic\n\t\t\t\t\t15788 text ,  from tests 65, 71, and June 2007.\n\t\t\t\t\t15789 text The LR question types that most often would prompt us to consider diagramming the Conditional Logic are \ufeff\n\t\t\t\t\t15790 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15791 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15792 text • Must Be True\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15793 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15794 text • Most Supported\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15795 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15796 text • Sufficient Assumption\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15797 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15798 text • Parallel / Parallel Flaw\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15799 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15800 text • Principle-Strengthen\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15801 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15802 text • Principle-Conform\n\t\t\t\t15803 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15804 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15805 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15806 text • Look out for conditional trigger words. \n\t\t\t\t\t15807 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15808 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15809 text • Practice diagramming some of them on your paper. \n\t\t\t\t\t15810 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15811 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15812 text • Look for conditionals that could chain together. \n\t\t\t\t\t15813 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15814 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15815 text • On Flaw questions with conditional logic, look for authors to abuse conditional logic with illegal reversals or negations.\n\t\t\t\t15816 image Parallel Flaw - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15817 heading Parallel Flaw - Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15818 text Parallel Flaw - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15819 1\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15831 text Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15832 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15833 text Get 4 out of 5 correct,\n\t\t\t\t\t15834 text to pass this Level.\n\t\t\t\t15835 image Principle-Conform: Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15836 heading Principle-Conform: Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15837 text Principle-Conform: Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15838 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t15839 text 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t15840 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15841 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15842 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15843 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15844 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15845 text There are three varieties of \n\t\t\t\t\t15846 text Principle-Conform\n\t\t\t\t\t15847 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15848 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15849 text • The stimulus is a principle (or pair of principles)\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15850 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15851 text • The answers are principles\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15852 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15853 text • There are no explicit principles, just implied/illustrated ones\n\t\t\t\t\t15854 text Principles in Stimulus\n\t\t\t\t\t15855 text When the stimulus is providing an explicit principle (or two), we\'re usually being tested on our ability to apply a conditional rule. \n\t\t\t\t\t15856 text To find an answer that Conforms to this principle, we want an answer where the situation described matches the Trigger of the principle, and the judgment concluded matches the Outcome of the principle. (Even when the principles aren\'t expressed as conditionals, there will still usually be two things we need to make sure match up).\n\t\t\t\t\t15857 text Principles in Answers\n\t\t\t\t\t15858 text It\'s essentially the same mindset as a Principle-Strengthen question. We read the argument and then anticipate the principle underlying the argument by pre-phrasing "IF evidence, THEN conclusion". We expect the correct answer to \n\t\t\t\t\t15859 text Link \n\t\t\t\t\t15860 text language from the Evidence to the Conclusion\'s language.\xa0All that\'s different is that because the question stem says \n\t\t\t\t\t15861 text conform \n\t\t\t\t\t15862 text to the author\'s reasoning, we can\'t pick an answer that\'s overly strong. (That usually doesn\'t matter, but occasionally it does)\n\t\t\t\t\t15863 text Implicit Principles\n\t\t\t\t\t15864 text These feel similar to Parallel reasoning questions, because we\'re given an argument in the stimulus, and then each answer choice is its own argument on its own unique topic. We\'re looking for an underlying similarity to connect the correct answer to the original argument.\n\t\t\t\t\t15865 text On Parallel questions, those similarities come more in the form of technical / structural similarities (i.e. "Since the original argument had a \n\t\t\t\t\t15866 text Most \n\t\t\t\t\t15867 text premise and a \n\t\t\t\t\t15868 text Some \n\t\t\t\t\t15869 text premise, the correct answer\'s argument will also have those features").\n\t\t\t\t\t15870 text But with Principle-Conform it\'s more about the underlying gist or rule-of-thumb. We don\'t try to diagram the arguments. We just want to articulate a general moral to the story or operating principle that\'s guiding the author\'s thinking, and then we try to find an answer that matches that.\n\t\t\t\t15871 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15872 text Get 4 of your last 5 correct, \n\t\t\t\t\t15873 text untimed\n\t\t\t\t\t15874 text , to pass this \n\t\t\t\t\t15875 text level\n\t\t\t\t\t15876 text .\n\t\t\t\t15877 image Speed Drill - Level 2\n\t\t\t\t15878 heading Speed Drill - Level 2, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15879 text Speed Drill - Level 2\n\t\t\t\t15880 text Pacing\n\t\t\t\t15881 text 45 mins\n\t\t\t\t15882 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15883 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15884 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15885 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15886 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15887 text This is a trio of \n\t\t\t\t\t15888 text level 2\n\t\t\t\t\t15889 text  passages from tests 62, 64, 69. There\'s a \n\t\t\t\t\t15890 text Present Debate\n\t\t\t\t\t15891 text , an \n\t\t\t\t\t15892 text Old / New\n\t\t\t\t\t15893 text , and a \n\t\t\t\t\t15894 text Problem / Solution\n\t\t\t\t\t15895 text  passage, although you could probably see all three as Problem / Solution, if you prefer.\n\t\t\t\t\t15896 text The goal of this exercise is to practice a sustained, brisk "speedwalking" pace. When the test is offering us its easier items, we need to act like it.\n\t\t\t\t\t15897 text We need to try pushing our pace so that we can bank some extra time to spend on the hardest parts of a section.\n\t\t\t\t15898 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15899 text Set yourself an appropriate time limit.\n\t\t\t\t\t15900 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15901 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15902 text • If you aren\'t yet used to finishing all four passages with enough time, give yourself  27  mins for this threesome. \n\t\t\t\t\t15903 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15904 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15905 text • If you tend to get through all four, then try doing them in  22  mins. \n\t\t\t\t\t15906 text Either way, keep your eye on the clock and have a guess for all 21 Q\'s (even if it\'s a blind guess). \n\t\t\t\t\t15907 text The time limit is supposed to force us into experimenting with new behaviors:\n\t\t\t\t\t15908 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15909 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15910 text • when you have high confidence about an answer choice, pick it and move on without worrying about reading all the other answers you haven\'t seen yet. (high confidence comes when we find an answer choice that matches the  meaning  of a line in the passage, but an exact  language  match usually means a trap answer. but  doesn\'t  match up with language in the passage, but we can tell LSAT has put some work into disguising it with synonyms or different syntax. \n\t\t\t\t\t15911 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15912 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15913 text • if you get four or five words into an answer choice and already see something you don\'t like, get out of there. we need to conserve time and mental energy by not processing the full sentence of every answer choice. find  earlier  reasons to disqualify an answer.\n\t\t\t\t\t15914 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15915 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15916 text • get the passage read in 2.5 minutes or less. be content to simply determine the topic and framework, find the ideas that fill your framework boxes, and don\'t worry about grabbing too much else. Read the first paragraph carefully, and read the 1st sentence of other paragraphs carefully, and read any  pivot  sentences ( but, yet, however ) carefully. Let the rest of it breeze by.\n\t\t\t\t\t15917 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15918 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15919 text • skip the worst problem in each passage set. we will tend to overspend time on that even though we have a lower average accuracy on that problem, so it\'s a bad value.\n\t\t\t\t\t15920 text Hit SUBMIT SET when the timer runs out. Then take a 2nd untimed look at the questions and explanations.\n\t\t\t\t15921 image Role - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15922 heading Role - Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15923 text Role - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15924 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t15925 text 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t15926 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15927 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15928 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15929 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15930 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15931 text On harder \n\t\t\t\t\t15932 text Role \n\t\t\t\t\t15933 text questions, we\'re likely to see a couple patterns emerge:\n\t\t\t\t\t15934 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15935 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15936 text • Intermediate Conclusion?  Many of the harder problems test the existence of an Intermediate Conclusion, even if the claim we\'re being asked about isn\'t itself that. Answer choices describing a Premise might differ by saying, "It\'s provides direct support for the Conclusion" vs. "It provide support for a claim that then provides direct support for the Conclusion".\n\t\t\t\t\t15937 text To assess whether a claim is or isn\'t an Intermediate Conclusion, we want to ask ourselves, "\n\t\t\t\t\t15938 text Is there\n\t\t\t\t\t15939 text Support\n\t\t\t\t\t15940 text  for this claim? Why should we believe this claim? Does anything else in the paragraph sound like it\'s answering that question?"\n\t\t\t\t\t15941 text Often, when there \n\t\t\t\t\t15942 text isn\'t \n\t\t\t\t\t15943 text a supporting idea present and thus the claim you\'re examining is really just a Premise, it\'s useful to think about how \n\t\t\t\t\t15944 text you\n\t\t\t\t\t15945 text would support that claim.\n\t\t\t\t\t15946 text If you\'re asking yourself, "Was the claim \n\t\t\t\t\t15947 text You shouldn\'t tell jokes at a funeral \n\t\t\t\t\t15948 text supported?" Supply your own answer, just get your brain hearing what actual support would sound like:\xa0\xa0"you shouldn\'t tell jokes at a funeral \n\t\t\t\t\t15949 text because\n\t\t\t\t\t15950 text ... funerals are a somber occasion and telling jokes makes it seem like you\'re not respecting the gravity of the situation". By articulating what support would sound like, you can sometimes help strengthen your conviction that no support was provided, if you\'re not seeing any claims like that.\n\t\t\t\t\t15951 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15952 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15953 text • Relational language, rather than classic Argument Role language.  Harder problems tend to supply fewer answers with recognizable terms like "Premise, Conclusion, Intermediate Conclusion" and either use more complicated abstract phrases to signify the same idea, or they don\'t really concern themselves with those labels at all. Instead, they just conversationally describe how the claims relate to each other, almost more like a  Method  of reasoning question. \n\t\t\t\t15954 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15955 text Get 4 out of your last 5 correct,\n\t\t\t\t\t15956 text to pass this level.\n\t\t\t\t15957 image Speedwalking LR (set 2)\n\t\t\t\t15958 heading Speedwalking LR (set 2), Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15959 text Speedwalking LR (set 2)\n\t\t\t\t15960 text Pacing\n\t\t\t\t15961 text 45 mins\n\t\t\t\t15962 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15963 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15964 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15965 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15966 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15967 text LENGTH\n\t\t\t\t\t15968 text  -- 15 Q\'s, 15 minutes (1.5x = 22, 2x = 30)\n\t\t\t\t\t15969 text TYPES\n\t\t\t\t\t15970 text  -- Paradox, Flaw, Role, Main Conclusion, Necessary Assumption, Sufficient Assumption, Strengthen, Weaken, Method, and Must Be True.\n\t\t\t\t\t15971 text LEVEL\n\t\t\t\t\t15972 text  -- 1\n\t\t\t\t\t15973 text Wait a sec -- these are all level 1? I thought this activity was listed as level 5?\n\t\t\t\t\t15974 text Yes, because the goal is something a level 5 student needs to work on:\xa0\xa0be able to quickly take care of easier questions, so that you\'ll have more time and brainpower in reserves for the harder, more flexible thinking questions in the section.\n\t\t\t\t\t15975 text Given how many subtle reading traps there are on LSAT, it\'s sometimes difficult to ever let yourself believe that an answer you find appealing is correct. "It\'s never this easy", we might think. But, sure it is! Sometimes it really is that easy. We need to improve our ability to \n\t\t\t\t\t15976 text let the easy be easy\n\t\t\t\t\t15977 text .\n\t\t\t\t\t15978 text And we need to develop enough self-trust while we\'re doing easier problems that we can pick up our pace when possible.\n\t\t\t\t15979 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15980 text Try to get through these 15 questions in 15 mins. Keep yourself going at a brisk pace. When you have a strong idea of what you\'re looking for (like on Main Conclusion, Role, Sufficient Assumption, Flaw), try to be proactive about scanning for and finding your answer, rather than reading all five choices start to finish.\n\t\t\t\t\t15981 text However, on tasks where we compare the impact of new information (like Paradox, Strengthen, Weaken), we may still need to use more time to consider all five answers.\n\t\t\t\t\t15982 text If your thinking feels unfinished on any of them, flag them as you go (so that you can maintain your brisk pace), and then take a second look at them after the timer goes off before you check your answer / the explanation.\n\t\t\t\t15983 image PrepTest 141 - Section 3\n\t\t\t\t15984 heading PrepTest 141 - Section 3, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15985 text PrepTest 141 - Section 3\n\t\t\t\t15986 text Timed Section 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t15987 button Take Section\n\t\t\t\t\t15988 text Take Section\n\t\t\t\t15989 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15990 image PrepTest 143 - Section 1\n\t\t\t\t15991 heading PrepTest 143 - Section 1, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15992 text PrepTest 143 - Section 1\n\t\t\t\t15993 text Timed Section 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t15994 button Take Section\n\t\t\t\t\t15995 text Take Section\n\t\t\t\t15996 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15997 image PrepTest 156\n\t\t\t\t15998 heading PrepTest 156, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15999 text PrepTest 156\n\t\t\t\t16000 text Practice Test 4 hrs, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t16001 button Take Test\n\t\t\t\t\t16002 text Take Test\n\t\t\t\t16003 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t16004 button \uf2c2\n\t\t\t\t\t16005 text \uf2c2\n\t\t\t16006 container\n\t\t\t\t16007 heading Week 15, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t16008 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t16009 text Week  15\n\t\t\t\t16010 text January 3rd - 9th, 2027\n\t\t\t\t16011 text Est. Time Remaining:  7 hrs, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t16012 text \uf113\n\t\t\t\t16013 image PrepTest 142 - Section 3\n\t\t\t\t16014 heading PrepTest 142 - Section 3, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t16015 text PrepTest 142 - Section 3\n\t\t\t\t16016 text Timed Section 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t16017 button Take Section\n\t\t\t\t\t16018 text Take Section\n\t\t\t\t16019 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t16020 image PrepTest 143 - Section 3\n\t\t\t\t16021 heading PrepTest 143 - Section 3, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t16022 text PrepTest 143 - Section 3\n\t\t\t\t16023 text Timed Section 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t16024 button Take Section\n\t\t\t\t\t16025 text Take Section\n\t\t\t\t16026 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t16027 image PrepTest 158\n\t\t\t\t16028 heading PrepTest 158, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t16029 text PrepTest 158\n\t\t\t\t16030 text Practice Test 4 hrs, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t16031 button Take Test\n\t\t\t\t\t16032 text Take Test\n\t\t\t\t16033 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t16034 button \uf2c2\n\t\t\t\t\t16035 text \uf2c2\n\t\t\t16036 container\n\t\t\t\t16037 heading Week 16, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t16038 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t16039 text Week  16\n\t\t\t\t16040 text January 10th - 16th, 2027\n\t\t\t\t16041 text Est. Time Remaining:  8 hrs, 22 mins\n\t\t\t\t45 text \uf113\n\t\t\t\t46 image How to Use LSAT Lab\n\t\t\t\t47 heading How to Use LSAT Lab, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t48 text How to Use LSAT Lab\n\t\t\t\t49 text Video\n\t\t\t\t50 text 16 mins\n\t\t\t\t51 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t52 text Info\n\t\t\t\t53 button Watch\n\t\t\t\t\t54 text Watch\n\t\t\t\t55 button Finish\n\t\t\t\t\t56 text Finish\n\t\t\t\t57 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t58 text This is a video overview of how to use the site. \n\t\t\t\t59 image Dissecting Arguments\n\t\t\t\t60 heading Dissecting Arguments, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t61 text Dissecting Arguments\n\t\t\t\t62 text Video\n\t\t\t\t63 text 40 mins Completed\n\t\t\t\t64 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t65 text Info\n\t\t\t\t66 button Watch\n\t\t\t\t\t67 text Watch\n\t\t\t\t68 button Takeaways\n\t\t\t\t\t69 text Takeaways\n\t\t\t\t70 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t71 container\n\t\t\t\t\t72 text In this 30 minute lesson, we\'ll define the ingredients of arguments and tell you the common keywords used with each type of ingredient. \n\t\t\t\t\t73 text Then we\'ll read through a dozen arguments, to practice dissecting them into Conclusions, Premises, and other types of claims.\n\t\t\t\t74 text Watch the video, pausing it when indicated so that you can do your own analysis before you hear ours.\n\t\t\t\t75 image Find the Conclusion\n\t\t\t\t76 heading Find the Conclusion, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t77 text Find the Conclusion\n\t\t\t\t78 text Flashcards\n\t\t\t\t79 text 10 mins\n\t\t\t\t80 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t81 text Info\n\t\t\t\t82 link Description: Start, Value: app.lsatlab.com/fla…\n\t\t\t\t83 button Finish\n\t\t\t\t\t84 text Finish\n\t\t\t\t85 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t86 container\n\t\t\t\t\t87 text ~70% of the paragraphs we read in LR are labeled \n\t\t\t\t\t88 text arguments\n\t\t\t\t\t89 text  or \n\t\t\t\t\t90 text reasoning. \n\t\t\t\t\t91 text What do those words mean? \n\t\t\t\t\t92 text A claim  that is \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0supported by some  other claim (s)\n\t\t\t\t\t93 text \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Conclusion\n\t\t\t\t\t94 text Evidence, Premise, Support\n\t\t\t\t\t95 text ____________________________________________________________________\n\t\t\t\t\t96 text To analyze an argument (which we do on 70% of LR questions), our first step is to find the Conclusion and its Supporting Idea(s). In most cases there is more than one Supporting Idea, but often there is only one premise. In a small percent of cases, there is more than one Conclusion. In those cases, there is a Main Conclusion that is supported by an Intermediate Conclusion, which is supported by its own premise.  ____________________________________________________________________\n\t\t\t\t\t97 text THE CONCLUSION TESTS\n\t\t\t\t\t98 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t99 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t100 text • Is it\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t101 text supported\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t102 text by some other claim?\n\t\t\t\t\t103 text (If we\'re looking at a Conclusion and we ask, "\n\t\t\t\t\t104 text Why should I believe that?\n\t\t\t\t\t105 text ", we will be able to point to at least one explicit supporting idea in the stimulus.)\n\t\t\t\t\t106 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t107 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t108 text • Is it the  author\'s opinion ?\n\t\t\t\t\t109 text (Factual claims and other people\'s opinions are almost never conclusions)\n\t\t\t\t\t110 text Note: to say that a claim is supported doesn\'t mean the argument \n\t\t\t\t\t111 text proved \n\t\t\t\t\t112 text the claim. The support doesn\'t have to be compelling or dispositive (fancy legal word meaning \n\t\t\t\t\t113 text it definitively settles the matter\n\t\t\t\t\t114 text ). It just has to feel like an idea the author thinks will help persuade us of her conclusion.  ____________________________________________________________________\n\t\t\t\t\t115 heading Use keywords whenever possible. , Value: 4\n\t\t\t\t\t\t116 text Use \n\t\t\t\t\t\t117 text keywords\n\t\t\t\t\t\t118 text  whenever possible. \n\t\t\t\t\t119 heading   , Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t120 text CONCLUSION: \n\t\t\t\t\t121 text so, thus, therefore, hence, it follows\n\t\t\t\t\t122 text PIVOT: \n\t\t\t\t\t123 text but, yet, however\n\t\t\t\t\t124 text OPINION: \n\t\t\t\t\t125 text clearly, obviously, should, probably, evidently\n\t\t\t\t\t126 text SUPPORT: \n\t\t\t\t\t127 text  (F.A.B.S.) for, after all, because, since\n\t\t\t\t\t128 text Support words \n\t\t\t\t\t129 text indirectly\n\t\t\t\t\t130 text  show us the Conclusion. The Conclusion is next door to them. If a claim is prefaced by FABS (for, after all, because, since), then it is  Support  for a  Conclusion  that came right before or right after.\n\t\t\t\t\t131 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t132 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t133 text • Since you like tea,  you should try boba.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t134 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t135 text • You should try boba.  because you like tea. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t136 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t137 text • You should try boba.  After all,  you like tea. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t138 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t139 text • You should try boba,  for  you like tea. \n\t\t\t\t140 container\n\t\t\t\t\t141 text Take \n\t\t\t\t\t142 text 7 minutes\n\t\t\t\t\t143 text  to try these flashcards.\n\t\t\t\t\t144 text Read each argument and \n\t\t\t\t\t145 text identify\n\t\t\t\t\t146 text  which of its explicit claims would be the \n\t\t\t\t\t147 text Main Conclusion\n\t\t\t\t\t148 text .\n\t\t\t\t149 image First Sentence Conclusions\n\t\t\t\t150 heading First Sentence Conclusions, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t151 text First Sentence Conclusions\n\t\t\t\t152 text Patterns\n\t\t\t\t153 text 22 mins\n\t\t\t\t154 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t155 text Info\n\t\t\t\t156 link Description: Continue, Value: app.lsatlab.com/pra…\n\t\t\t\t157 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t158 container\n\t\t\t\t\t159 text These six questions all have a \n\t\t\t\t\t160 text Conclusion\n\t\t\t\t\t161 text  in the \n\t\t\t\t\t162 text first sentence\n\t\t\t\t\t163 text , \n\t\t\t\t\t164 text which of course is not the most obvious place to find a conclusion. \n\t\t\t\t\t165 text But \n\t\t\t\t\t166 text that\'s the point\n\t\t\t\t\t167 text ! \n\t\t\t\t\t168 text When we\'re doing \n\t\t\t\t\t169 text Main Conclusion\n\t\t\t\t\t170 text  and \n\t\t\t\t\t171 text Role\n\t\t\t\t\t172 text  questions, the test writers are intentionally trying to hide the conclusion, so that this otherwise-easy task can still be challenging.\n\t\t\t\t\t173 text The most common place to find the conclusion is after a Pivot, expressing some Rebuttal sentiment (65% of Main Conclusion questions).\n\t\t\t\t\t174 text The second most common place they\'ll stash it is in the first sentence (25% of Main Conclusion questions).\n\t\t\t\t\t175 text Only about 20% of the time on Main Conclusion does the paragraph end with the conclusion. That\'s why picking an answer that matches the final claim will usually be wrong (but not always!)\n\t\t\t\t\t176 text We want to practice reading Main Conclusion questions with a special ear for "upside-down" arguments, where we hear the conclusion and \n\t\t\t\t\t177 text then \n\t\t\t\t\t178 text hear the supporting ideas. \n\t\t\t\t179 container\n\t\t\t\t\t180 text Try these six questions,\n\t\t\t\t\t181 text focusing on how we\'d know that the 1st sentence is the conclusion.\n\t\t\t\t\t182 text ____________________________________________________________________\n\t\t\t\t\t183 text This exercise is about getting our brains used to the feel of a pattern. Focus on noticing how the first claim is an \n\t\t\t\t\t184 text opinion\n\t\t\t\t\t185 text , and then \n\t\t\t\t\t186 text feeling \n\t\t\t\t\t187 text how the subsequent claims go on to defend that initial opinion.\n\t\t\t\t\t188 text Are there any \n\t\t\t\t\t189 text Support Indicator\n\t\t\t\t\t190 text  words that follow it?  (f.e. \n\t\t\t\t\t191 text FABS\n\t\t\t\t\t192 text  = for, after all, because, since) \n\t\t\t\t\t193 text Are there any \n\t\t\t\t\t194 text Opinion Indicator\n\t\t\t\t\t195 text  words in it?  (f.e. should, ought, probably, better) \n\t\t\t\t\t196 text If we look at the claim in the first sentence and ask ourselves, "\n\t\t\t\t\t197 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t198 text Why should we believe  that\n\t\t\t\t\t199 text ?", does the rest of an argument seem like an answer to that question? (it should)\n\t\t\t\t200 image Main Conclusion - Level 1\n\t\t\t\t201 heading Main Conclusion - Level 1, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t202 text Main Conclusion - Level 1\n\t\t\t\t203 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t204 text 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t205 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t206 text Info\n\t\t\t\t207 link Description: Start, Value: app.lsatlab.com/pra…\n\t\t\t\t208 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t209 container\n\t\t\t\t\t210 text reading goal\n\t\t\t\t\t211 text Find the conclusion.\n\t\t\t\t\t212 text Make sure that it\n\t\t\t\t\t213 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t214 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t215 text a . sounds like  Author\'s Opinion  (facts ≠ conclusions)\n\t\t\t\t\t\t216 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t217 text b . is  Supported  by at least one explicit claim.\n\t\t\t\t\t218 text stimulus tendencies\n\t\t\t\t\t219 text LSAC is seeking to make it harder than usual to find the Conclusion. Be aware that there will often be Intermediate Conclusions in these arguments that use obvious conclusion keywords. But the main conclusion usually isn\'t well-advertised like that. On this question type (and on Role), it\'s very rare to see the Conclusion be the final claim, prefaced by anything obvious like Therefore / Thus / So.\n\t\t\t\t\t220 text Instead, in more than 90% of Main Conclusion questions, \n\t\t\t\t\t221 text the Conclusion appears \n\t\t\t\t\t222 text earlier \n\t\t\t\t\t223 text than (at least some of) the Support.\n\t\t\t\t\t224 text These are the two most common places they stash the conclusion:\n\t\t\t\t\t225 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t226 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t227 text • First sentence\n\t\t\t\t\t\t228 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t229 text • after a  But / Yet / However  pivot\n\t\t\t\t230 container\n\t\t\t\t\t231 text Get 4 out of your last 5 correct,\n\t\t\t\t\t232 text to pass this Level for \n\t\t\t\t\t233 text Main Conclusion\n\t\t\t\t\t234 text correct answer\n\t\t\t\t\t235 text The correct answer just reproduces the meaning of the Conclusion. Sometimes it\'s a verbatim regurgitation. More commonly, they use synonyms or inverted syntax to present an equivalent meaning that still looks a little different.\n\t\t\t\t\t236 text f.e. if the conclusion appeared in the argument as "not all tornadoes should be avoided", then an equivalent claim would be "some tornadoes should not be avoided".\n\t\t\t\t\t237 text If you didn\'t already do the \n\t\t\t\t\t238 text 2-part Conclusion Check \n\t\t\t\t\t239 text when you were first reading the argument and determining which claim is the conclusion, you can do it now (or again) --\n\t\t\t\t\t240 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t241 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t242 text • is this answer expressing an  Opinion  from our Author? paragraph, and visualizing it as an argument\n\t\t\t\t\t258 text An \n\t\t\t\t\t259 text argument \n\t\t\t\t\t260 text is composed of a \n\t\t\t\t\t261 text Conclusion\n\t\t\t\t\t262 text  (usually opinionated) that is supported by at least one piece of \n\t\t\t\t\t263 text Evidence\n\t\t\t\t\t264 text  (i.e. Premise). \n\t\t\t\t\t265 text When we\'re reading arguments in LR (which is about 80% of the time), our first job is to separate out the Main Conclusion from its support (which could include Intermediate Conclusions). \n\t\t\t\t266 container\n\t\t\t\t\t267 text Practice finding via the \n\t\t\t\t\t322 text Challenge Position \n\t\t\t\t\t323 text framework what the author\'s emphasis and purpose were.\n\t\t\t\t324 container\n\t\t\t\t\t325 text Attempt the passages and questions \n\t\t\t\t\t326 text untimed\n\t\t\t\t\t327 text . \n\t\t\t\t\t328 text We\'ve already warned you that you can use a Challenge Position framework, so pay a lot of attention to where we see some Position(s) early on, attributed to someone other than the Author. \n\t\t\t\t\t329 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t330 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t331 text • Does she provide any clues along the way that or give it any faint praise like "somewhat plausibly / seemingly true / sounds reasonable"?\n\t\t\t\t\t335 text Usually, the pivot into the author\'s \n\t\t\t\t\t336 text Challenge\n\t\t\t\t\t337 text  is introduced with a classic \n\t\t\t\t\t338 text But / Yet / However\n\t\t\t\t\t339 text .\n\t\t\t\t340 image Dumb This Down\n\t\t\t\t341 heading Dumb This Down, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t342 text Dumb easier, simple language (use slang, examples, metaphor, if possible).\n\t\t\t\t353 container\n\t\t\t\t\t354 text Set a timer for 10 mins. \n\t\t\t\t\t355 text For each of these cards, try saying / writing / typing your own dumbed down version of the text before you look at our version.\n\t\t\t\t\t356 text Some of them use actual RC excerpts. Other cards take a famous expression like, "You never get a second chance to make a first impression" and turn it into LSAT prose, like, "Fostering an initial assessment in someone is an opportunity that can\'t be replicated."\n\t\t\t\t357 image Rebuttals\n\t\t\t\t358 heading Rebuttals, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t359 text Rebuttals\n\t\t\t\t360 text Video\n\t\t\t\t361 text 50 mins Completed\n\t\t\t\t362 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t363 text Info\n\t\t\t\t364 button Watch\n\t\t\t\t\t365 text Watch\n\t\t\t\t366 button Takeaways\n\t\t\t\t\t367 text Takeaways\n\t\t\t\t368 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t369 container\n\t\t\t\t\t370 text Many arguments in the Logical Reasoning section have a \n\t\t\t\t\t371 text rebuttal \n\t\t\t\t\t372 text structure. The argument opens with (or implies) some other point of view.\n\t\t\t\t\t373 text We typically see \n\t\t\t\t\t374 text attribution \n\t\t\t\t\t375 text language early on, such as:\n\t\t\t\t\t376 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t377 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t378 text • many people think that\n\t\t\t\t\t\t379 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t380 text • some psychologists say that\n\t\t\t\t\t\t381 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t382 text • it is commonly assumed that\n\t\t\t\t\t383 text This is typically followed by a \n\t\t\t\t\t384 text pivot\n\t\t\t\t\t385 text : but, yet, however\n\t\t\t\t\t386 text Pivots represent a turning point in the argument from the background/counterpoint to the author\'s actual argument. From there we have to figure out which claim is the support, which is the conclusion.\n\t\t\t\t\t387 text We also want to articulate the rebuttal conclusion. For example, if we read, "Many people think the sun is predominantly iron. But they\'re wrong", we don\'t want to think of the Conclusion as "\n\t\t\t\t\t388 text They\'re wrong\n\t\t\t\t\t389 text ". We want to articulate that the author\'s conclusion is saying, "the Sun is \n\t\t\t\t\t390 text not \n\t\t\t\t\t391 text predominantly iron."\n\t\t\t\t392 container\n\t\t\t\t\t393 text Watch the video. Try to answer these questions:\n\t\t\t\t\t394 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t395 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t396 text • What sort of features are useful indicators of a Rebuttal style argument?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t397 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t398 text • What extra steps do we perform with the Conclusion?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t399 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t400 text • Which 2 of the 10 Famous Flaws are related to Rebuttals?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t401 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t402 text • What are the two most common places where the main conclusion is found on a Main Conclusion question?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t403 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t404 text • What should we keep in mind when we see a Rebuttal in a Most Supported context?\n\t\t\t\t405 image Dumb it Down\n\t\t\t\t406 heading Dumb it Down, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t407 text Dumb it Down\n\t\t\t\t408 text AI Skills Training\n\t\t\t\t409 text 10 mins\n\t\t\t\t410 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t411 text Info\n\t\t\t\t412 link Description: Start, Value: app.lsatlab.com/ski…\n\t\t\t\t413 button Finish\n\t\t\t\t\t414 text Finish\n\t\t\t\t415 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t416 container\n\t\t\t\t\t417 text The Core Skill of RC\n\t\t\t\t\t418 text When learning scientists do research onto what techniques give students the most boost when it comes to retaining a passage, the clear champion is \n\t\t\t\t\t419 text Self-Summarization\n\t\t\t\t\t420 text .\n\t\t\t\t\t421 text This has way more benefit than annotating, note-taking, previewing the questions first, etc.\n\t\t\t\t\t422 text When we highlight or take notes, we often freeze our attention on specific words the passage used, but LSAT is testing us on the \n\t\t\t\t\t423 text meaning \n\t\t\t\t\t424 text of those words, not the words themselves.\n\t\t\t\t\t425 text When we self-summarize, we actually convert those words into meaning. We also make that meaning easier to remember by using conversational, gossipy language and by condensing things down to their core idea.\n\t\t\t\t426 container\n\t\t\t\t\t427 text Fully-Baked Comprehension\n\t\t\t\t\t428 text Work on this skill of reading a paragraph of prose and then boiling it down to one core idea, stripping away academic language and putting it into plainspoken English, as though you\'re texting a one sentence summary of the paragraph to your friend.\n\t\t\t\t\t429 text It\'s almost impossible to reduce a whole paragraph into an effective, short synthesis without first understanding the purpose behind this paragraph. What does the author care most about you knowing, especially as it pertains to connecting to the next paragraph? \n\t\t\t\t430 image Rebuttal Conclusions\n\t\t\t\t431 heading Rebuttal Conclusions, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t432 text Rebuttal Conclusions\n\t\t\t\t433 text Patterns\n\t\t\t\t434 text 22 mins Completed\n\t\t\t\t435 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t436 text Info\n\t\t\t\t437 link Description: See Results, Value: app.lsatlab.com/pra…\n\t\t\t\t438 button Takeaways\n\t\t\t\t\t439 text Takeaways\n\t\t\t\t440 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t441 container\n\t\t\t\t\t442 text When we do \n\t\t\t\t\t443 text Main Conclusion \n\t\t\t\t\t444 text questions, we expect LSAT to avoid putting the conclusion in its most obvious place (the final claim). We also expect them to avoid using obvious conclusion indicators (like therefore, thus, hence, so). \n\t\t\t\t\t445 text Instead, we expect the conclusion to usually either be the \n\t\t\t\t\t446 text first claim\n\t\t\t\t\t447 text  or be some \n\t\t\t\t\t448 text rebuttal\n\t\t\t\t\t449 text , typically introduced with Pivot words like but, however, yet. \n\t\t\t\t\t450 text Rebuttal conclusions usually have some sort of pronoun or referential language -- e.g. "But \n\t\t\t\t\t451 text this plan \n\t\t\t\t\t452 text would be likely to fail", "However \n\t\t\t\t\t453 text her conclusion\n\t\t\t\t\t454 text  is misguided". We need to replace those pronouns / referential ideas in a conclusion with the actual ideas they map back to.\n\t\t\t\t455 container\n\t\t\t\t\t456 text Try these four \n\t\t\t\t\t457 text Main Conclusion\n\t\t\t\t\t458 text  questions, all of which involve arguments with rebuttal conclusions.\n\t\t\t\t459 image Rebuttal Rephrase\n\t\t\t\t460 heading Rebuttal Rephrase, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t461 text Rebuttal Rephrase\n\t\t\t\t462 text AI Skills Training\n\t\t\t\t463 text 10 mins\n\t\t\t\t464 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t465 text Info\n\t\t\t\t466 link Description: Start, Value: app.lsatlab.com/ski…\n\t\t\t\t467 button Finish\n\t\t\t\t\t468 text Finish\n\t\t\t\t469 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t470 container\n\t\t\t\t\t471 text Articulate the Rebuttal Conclusion\n\t\t\t\t\t472 text This is one of our nerdiest phrases. It sounds complicated, but it\'s a very easy idea. We\'re essentially just flipping the logical light switch on an idea. \n\t\t\t\t\t473 text EXAMPLE: Some people say that Lebron is the best basketball player ever. But they\'re wrong. After all, [evidence].\n\t\t\t\t\t474 text The conclusion is the sentence that says "They\'re wrong". But by itself it has no meaning. So we need to better articulate what the author means by rebutting "they\'re wrong".\n\t\t\t\t\t475 text BAD: They\'re wrong. BETTER: People are wrong to say that Lebron is the best basketball player ever. BEST: Lebron isn\'t the best basketball player ever.\n\t\t\t\t\t476 text We took the original attributed idea, "Lebron is the best", and just flipped its logical light switch to get "Lebron isn\'t the best".\n\t\t\t\t\t477 text This drill is about practicing that skill. \n\t\t\t\t478 container\n\t\t\t\t\t479 text Practice This Skill for 7 Minutes\n\t\t\t\t\t480 text You\'ll be given an argument that contains a rebuttal conclusion. Your job is to express what that conclusion means in specific wording. If the conclusion is using any sort of pronoun / referential wording (e.g. "\n\t\t\t\t\t481 text This \n\t\t\t\t\t482 text reasoning is misguided / \n\t\t\t\t\t483 text Such \n\t\t\t\t\t484 text actions will not produce \n\t\t\t\t\t485 text the intended effect\n\t\t\t\t\t486 text "), you\'ll need to import the specific wording into those referential words/phrases. And of course you\'ll need to flip the logical light switch on the idea.\n\t\t\t\t\t487 text Flipping the switch on the idea is essentially the same idea as negating an answer choice (as we do in Necessary Assumption), or negating conclusions when we\'re trying to argue the Anti-Conclusion perspective (as we do on Flaw, Weaken, and other question types). \n\t\t\t\t\t488 text Negating a claim means the same as "the \n\t\t\t\t\t489 text minimum \n\t\t\t\t\t490 text way to contradict this claim". (it has nothing to do with \n\t\t\t\t\t491 text illegal negations\n\t\t\t\t\t492 text  in conditional logic)\n\t\t\t\t\t493 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t494 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t495 text • When the truth value of a claim hinges on its  Quantifier , you negate that quantifier.\n\t\t\t\t\t496 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t497 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t498 text • When the truth value hinges on the Telling Part  not  being true, you negate the "not" by removing it.\n\t\t\t\t\t499 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t500 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t501 text • If it\'s a conditional claim, the truth value hinges on its certainty. It\'s saying something is Always true or true in All cases. So you negate the certainty / the universal / the guarantee. By claiming "it\'s not certain", we are claiming that "there is at least one counterexample" or "it\'s possible for the trigger to be true but the outcome to be false". \n\t\t\t\t\t502 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t503 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t504 text • For all other sentences, the truth value hinges on the verb, because the verb is what starts the Telling Part of the sentence. \n\t\t\t\t505 image Rebuttals Level 1\n\t\t\t\t506 heading Rebuttals Level 1, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t507 text Rebuttals Level 1\n\t\t\t\t508 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t509 text 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t510 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t511 text Info\n\t\t\t\t512 link Description: Start, Value: app.lsatlab.com/pra…\n\t\t\t\t513 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t514 container\n\t\t\t\t\t515 text Over 10% of questions in an LR section feature \n\t\t\t\t\t516 text Rebuttals\n\t\t\t\t\t517 text .\xa0\n\t\t\t\t\t518 text When we see a Rebuttal within a  1-speaker stimulus , usually that stimulus will have this structure: 1)\xa0An \n\t\t\t\t\t519 text Attributed\n\t\t\t\t\t520 text  Claim/Argument  (signified by wording like “Some people say / It is often assumed that / Many biologists think”)\xa0\n\t\t\t\t\t521 text 2) A \n\t\t\t\t\t522 text Pivot\n\t\t\t\t\t523 text (such as “but / yet / however”)\n\t\t\t\t\t524 text 3) A \n\t\t\t\t\t525 text Disagreement\n\t\t\t\t\t526 text  (make sure to differentiate between harsh rebuttals like “This claim is false” and softer rebuttals like “This reasoning is faulty”. Many times authors are saying that the current evidence doesn’t prove the conclusion, but they’re not actually claiming that the conclusion is a false claim.)\n\t\t\t\t\t527 text 4) The \n\t\t\t\t\t528 text Author’s Evidence\n\t\t\t\t\t529 text  (they’re often showing that a strong claim is false by pointing to a putative counterexample, or they’re showing that a hypothesis is unproven by pointing to a potential alternate explanation for the opposing evidence).\xa0\n\t\t\t\t\t530 text The other common variation is for the Author\'s Disagreement to have the opposing position embedded. For example, an argument might start this way: Crime is down 20% this year. However, it would be a mistake to credit this change to more aggressive policing. After all, ... \n\t\t\t\t\t531 text We can see in that 2nd sentence that the opposing position is, "Crime is down because of more aggressive policing."\n\t\t\t\t\t532 text In either case, the most important step in most questions involving rebuttals is to \n\t\t\t\t\t533 text Articulate the Rebuttal Conclusion\n\t\t\t\t\t534 text . \n\t\t\t\t\t535 text In the previous example that would mean saying to ourselves, "The author is concluding that \n\t\t\t\t\t536 text Crime is \n\t\t\t\t\t537 text not\n\t\t\t\t\t538 text  down because of aggressive policing\n\t\t\t\t\t539 text ." \n\t\t\t\t\t540 text When a Rebuttal involves a  2-speaker stimulus , usually the second person will be undermining the first person’s reasoning by pointing to an \n\t\t\t\t\t541 text Alternate Explanation\n\t\t\t\t\t542 text  for their evidence,\xa0by pointing to a \n\t\t\t\t\t543 text Distinction \n\t\t\t\t\t544 text or \n\t\t\t\t\t545 text Counterexample\n\t\t\t\t\t546 text  that goes against what the author was saying, or by showing that the first person\'s claim or plan has \n\t\t\t\t\t547 text Faulty Implications\n\t\t\t\t\t548 text . \n\t\t\t\t549 container\n\t\t\t\t\t550 heading Get 4 out of 5 correct , Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t551 text Get 4 out of 5 correct \n\t\t\t\t\t552 heading to pass this level., Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t553 text to pass this level.\n\t\t\t\t\t554 text In \n\t\t\t\t\t555 text Main Conclusion \n\t\t\t\t\t556 text and \n\t\t\t\t\t557 text Role \n\t\t\t\t\t558 text questions, most conclusions are found \n\t\t\t\t\t559 text earlier \n\t\t\t\t\t560 text than the supporting ideas. About 60% of conclusions on Main Conclusion are some sort of Rebuttal claim.\n\t\t\t\t\t561 text On \n\t\t\t\t\t562 text Method\n\t\t\t\t\t563 text , there are four common forms of rebuttal:\n\t\t\t\t\t564 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t565 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t566 text • suggest the first person is making a dubious assumption\n\t\t\t\t\t\t567 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t568 text • point out faulty implications / consequences of their claim or plan\n\t\t\t\t\t\t569 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t570 text • suggest an alternate explanation for their evidence\n\t\t\t\t\t\t571 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t572 text • point out a distinction or counterexample\n\t\t\t\t\t573 text On \n\t\t\t\t\t574 text Flaw\n\t\t\t\t\t575 text , two of the 10 famous flaws relate to rebuttals:\n\t\t\t\t\t576 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t577 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t578 text • Ad Hominem :\xa0\xa0the author dismisses a view because the source is biased or has some hypocritical/conflicting behavior or beliefs.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t579 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t580 text • Unproven vs. Proven False :\xa0\xa0the author cites someone\'s failure to prove X (either because they lack evidence or because they made a faulty argument in favor of X) and then concludes that X is false.\n\t\t\t\t\t581 text On \n\t\t\t\t\t582 text Fill in the Blank\n\t\t\t\t\t583 text , if we see a rebuttal structure, the correct answer will usually sound like a Rebuttal conclusion, but trap answers will try to entice us into a too-strong version of that conclusion.\n\t\t\t\t584 image a Framework\n\t\t\t\t662 heading Find a Framework, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t663 text Find a Framework\n\t\t\t\t664 text Video\n\t\t\t\t665 text 30 mins Completed\n\t\t\t\t666 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t667 text Info\n\t\t\t\t668 button Watch\n\t\t\t\t\t669 text Watch\n\t\t\t\t670 button Takeaways\n\t\t\t\t\t671 text Takeaways\n\t\t\t\t672 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t673 container\n\t\t\t\t\t674 text This 30 minute animated lesson introduces  the Top 5 \n\t\t\t\t\t675 text Frameworks\n\t\t\t\t\t676 text  for RC passages. \n\t\t\t\t\t677 text Frameworks are kind of like movie / literary genres. Within a genre or framework, you can have some reliable guesses about what the big moments will be and when they\'ll come.\n\t\t\t\t678 container\n\t\t\t\t\t679 text This video won\'t do much to change your brain unless you resolve to follow up on watching it by trying it on a couple passages. \n\t\t\t\t\t680 text \ufeffSo pay attention to what you\'re watching with the thought of, "Right after I watch this, I\'m spending 5-10 minutes reading some first paragraphs from some random RC passages and attempting to pick a framework."\n\t\t\t\t681 image Finding Frameworks (round 1)\n\t\t\t\t682 heading Finding Frameworks (round 1), Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t683 text Finding Frameworks (round 1)\n\t\t\t\t684 text Flashcards\n\t\t\t\t685 text 15 mins\n\t\t\t\t686 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t687 text Info\n\t\t\t\t688 link Description: Start, Value: app.lsatlab.com/fla…\n\t\t\t\t689 button Finish\n\t\t\t\t\t690 text Finish\n\t\t\t\t691 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t692 container\n\t\t\t\t\t693 text Reading the first paragraph, we want to feel like detectives. \n\t\t\t\t\t694 text We\'re taking in the meaning of the early sentences, but we\'re trying to solve a mystery:\n\t\t\t\t\t695 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t696 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t697 text • What is the central topic? \n\t\t\t\t\t\t698 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t699 text • Why is the author writing about it? \n\t\t\t\t\t\t700 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t701 text • Which of the big 5 (CHOPP) or 7 total frameworks (CHOPPIE) could we use to organize the big ideas in this passage?\n\t\t\t\t702 container\n\t\t\t\t\t703 text With each card, read the first paragraph and think about which framework(s) would seem usable. If there are multiple paragraphs, feel free to update your choice of Framework if the passage goes somewhere you weren\'t predicting.\n\t\t\t\t\t704 text Set a 10 minute timer\n\t\t\t\t\t705 text .  \ufeffWhen it\'s goes off, you\'re good to go, unless you\'re feeling like doing more. \n\t\t\t\t706 image Framework Sampler\n\t\t\t\t707 heading Framework Sampler, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t708 text Framework Sampler\n\t\t\t\t709 text Patterns\n\t\t\t\t710 text 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t711 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t712 text Info\n\t\t\t\t713 link Description: Start, Value: app.lsatlab.com/pra…\n\t\t\t\t714 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t715 container\n\t\t\t\t\t716 text This set contains \n\t\t\t\t\t717 text four RC passages\n\t\t\t\t\t718 text , each one with a different Framework.\n\t\t\t\t\t719 text There is an Old / New, a Problem / Solution, a Present Debate, and a Challenge Position, along with the Main Point or Primary Purpose question accompanying that passage.\n\t\t\t\t\t720 text Read each passage, trying to discern the Framework and reading for the Framework Fill-In\'s. Think about the main point through the lens of the author\'s purpose. \n\t\t\t\t\t721 text Why \n\t\t\t\t\t722 text is the author writing about this topic? These questions are all about initially understanding how the the paragraph is creating some cognitive dissonance (the feeling when two ideas don\'t fit well together), and then picking an answer that resolves that tension, and helps give us a way to understand how both things can be true. Most correct answers provide some important difference between two things, two groups, two timeframes, or two situations. Principle-Strengthen\n\t\t\t\t\t780 text read arguments and analyze their logical gaps / think about potential objections.\n\t\t\t\t\t781 text Match Family\n\t\t\t\t\t782 text Main Conclusion, Role, Method, Parallel, Parallel Flaw, Principle-Conform\n\t\t\t\t\t783 text read arguments, identifying and characterizing the separate parts of the argument as well as their relationships to each other.\n\t\t\t\t\t784 text Inference Family\n\t\t\t\t\t785 text must be true, must be false, most supported, agree/disagree\n\t\t\t\t\t786 text read statements and pick the answer that is most supportably derived from those statements.\n\t\t\t\t\t787 text Paradox\n\t\t\t\t\t788 text These questions don\'t belong in the first two families, because we aren\'t reading arguments. But they don\'t belong in the last family, because we aren\'t picking the idea that is most derivable/provable from the statements. The stronger the wording, the more impact an answer potentially has, so this is a question type where we \n\t\t\t\t\t890 text Prefer Stronger Language\n\t\t\t\t\t891 text , and where we could consider \n\t\t\t\t\t892 text Weak Language = Red Flag\n\t\t\t\t\t893 text  (sometimes, can, may, might, not all, not always). \n\t\t\t\t\t894 text But our task is \n\t\t\t\t\t895 text relative\n\t\t\t\t\t896 text ; it\'s on a sliding scale, meaning the correct answer just has to do \n\t\t\t\t\t897 text more \n\t\t\t\t\t898 text to help explain than any other answer. trying to find an answer where every ingredient matches up, and it takes us on a journey from the beginning to the ending of the passage. The short-cut we can often use to get rid of some answers quickly is by checking their last ingredient 1st. If the last ingredient doesn\'t match the ending of the passage, then the rest of the answer probably isn\'t worth reading.\n\t\t\t\t\t953 text (1) Primary Purpose\n\t\t\t\t\t954 text This type of question mainly wants us to answer in terms of what Framework we used, but of course LSAT isn\'t limited to using the 5-7 frameworks that we use\n\t\t\t\t955 container\n\t\t\t\t\t956 text Attempt the passages and questions \n\t\t\t\t\t957 text untimed\n\t\t\t\t\t958 text . \n\t\t\t\t\t959 text We\'ve already warned you that you can use a Challenge Position framework (but when an author is criticizing we can often also hear the possibility for Problem / Solution). \n\t\t\t\t\t960 text \ufeffSo pay a lot of attention to where we see an attribution to a different point of view early on, and encode that as the Position. They are essentially the same question type, but it\'s very common for people to do much better at one than the other, so they evidently feel different in people\'s brains. Weaken is often confused with Flaw, because the two have a lot of overlapping qualities. \n\t\t\t\t\t1011 text keywords\n\t\t\t\t\t1012 text weakens, undermines, casts doubt on, fails to consider, ignores the possibility\n\t\t\t\t\t1013 text examples\n\t\t\t\t\t1014 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t1015 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t1016 text • Which of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t1017 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t1018 text • Which of the following, if true, casts the most doubt on Tom\'s reasoning?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t1019 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t1020 text • The argument is most vulnerable to criticism because it fails to consider that\n\t\t\t\t\t1021 text (this last one could also be called a Flaw question, but technically the \n\t\t\t\t\t1022 text fails to consider\n\t\t\t\t\t1023 text  warns us that all the answer choices will be written in Weaken form)\n\t\t\t\t1024 container\n\t\t\t\t\t1025 text Watch this video lesson on \n\t\t\t\t\t1026 text Weaken\n\t\t\t\t\t1027 text questions.\n\t\t\t\t\t1028 text To evaluate answers, pretend that you are a judge or jury member, judging a trial between a prosecutor who is trying to convince you of \n\t\t\t\t\t1029 text Conclusion\n\t\t\t\t\t1030 text , and a defense lawyer who is trying to create some doubt about whether \n\t\t\t\t\t1031 text Conclusion \n\t\t\t\t\t1032 text is true or about whether the prosecutor\'s \n\t\t\t\t\t1033 text Evidence \n\t\t\t\t\t1034 text is compelling, relevant, or complete.\n\t\t\t\t\t1035 text With each answer, think to yourself, "Does this help the plaintiff\'s case? Does this help the defendant\'s case? Or is this idea neutral, irrelevant, or inadmissible to the trial we\'re having here today, which is only about whether or not \n\t\t\t\t\t1036 text Conclusion \n\t\t\t\t\t1037 text is true?"\n\t\t\t\t1038 image Weaken + Comparison\n\t\t\t\t1039 heading Weaken + Comparison, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t1040 text Weaken + Comparison\n\t\t\t\t1041 text Process\n\t\t\t\t1042 text 37 mins\n\t\t\t\t1043 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t1044 text Info\n\t\t\t\t1045 link Description: Continue, Value: app.lsatlab.com/pra…\n\t\t\t\t1046 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t1047 container\n\t\t\t\t\t1048 text COMPARISONS\n\t\t\t\t\t1049 text often lead us to  ask one of these two questions:\n\t\t\t\t\t1050 text 1. X→A  ..............  \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0B→Y  ....\n\t\t\t\t\t15224 text assumption\n\t\t\t\t15225 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15226 text Really difficult Sufficient Assumption questions usually work by having a correct answer that Rules Out Possible Objections or a correct answer that works in an unexpected way. \n\t\t\t\t\t15227 text Instead of finding an answer with the "perfect" missing link we were looking for, we might find a correct answer whose trigger is implied by the evidence but was not directly stated by the evidence.\n\t\t\t\t\t15228 text We might find a correct answer that helps us complete a "binary argument", meaning it has the flow of "If X is true, then we ultimately get to our conclusion. And if X is not true, then we still get to our conclusion."\n\t\t\t\t15229 image Oh, the Humanities! \n\t\t\t\t15230 heading Oh, the Humanities!, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15231 text Oh, the Humanities!\n\t\t\t\t15232 text Process\n\t\t\t\t15233 text 52 mins\n\t\t\t\t15234 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15235 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15236 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15237 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15238 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15239 text It\'s no accident that we invoked the famous quote from the fiery crash of the Hindenburg blimp. Each of these level 5 \n\t\t\t\t\t15240 text Humanities\n\t\t\t\t\t15241 text  passages brought down many students\' RC scores on tests 59 and 79.\n\t\t\t\t\t15242 text So buckle up for a challenge, mostly on the backend of trying to get all the questions correct. \n\t\t\t\t\t15243 text The most common frameworks for Humanities passages are \n\t\t\t\t\t15244 text Highlight Noteworthy\n\t\t\t\t\t15245 text  (a descriptive essay emphasizing the essence, motivation, or importance of an artist\'s style) and \n\t\t\t\t\t15246 text Challenge Position\n\t\t\t\t\t15247 text  (an essay that defends an artist against criticism or clarifies a misconception people have about them).\n\t\t\t\t15248 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15249 text Try these two passages, \n\t\t\t\t\t15250 text untimed\n\t\t\t\t\t15251 text seeing if you can figure out all the correct answers\n\t\t\t\t\t15252 text In both passages, students often struggle to fully understand the aesthetic concerns or design properties of the artists being profiled, and some of the questions in these passage sets are just downright tricky.\n\t\t\t\t\t15253 text In order to get them all right, you\'ll probably have to select a few answers you don\'t really like, but you will be reassuring yourself, "This answer seems weird, ... but I guess I\'d have to say that this answer is the \n\t\t\t\t\t15254 text best available \n\t\t\t\t\t15255 text option". \n\t\t\t\t15256 image Agree / Disagree - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15257 heading Agree / Disagree - Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15258 text Agree / Disagree - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15259 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t15260 text 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t15261 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15262 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15263 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15264 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15265 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15266 text Get 4 out of your last 5 correct to conquer  \ufeffLevel 5 for \n\t\t\t\t\t15267 text Agree / Disagree\n\t\t\t\t\t15268 text .\n\t\t\t\t15269 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15270 text Remember that Disagree problems are usually like doing \n\t\t\t\t\t15271 text two \n\t\t\t\t\t15272 text Most Supported questions at once:\n\t\t\t\t\t15273 text The correct answer choice should be a claim we can pretty much derive from one of the two speakers. The negation of that answer choice should be a claim we can pretty much derive from the other speaker.\n\t\t\t\t\t15274 text One sneaky move we see a lot on harder Agree / Disagree problems involves arguing over a conditional claim. By using restrictive, conditional wording, a person is technically commenting on a lot of stuff they never directly referred to.\n\t\t\t\t\t15275 text For example, if Kenny says, "Only well-painted canvases should be considered art", then we know his opinion on all these claims, even though Kenny never mentioned \n\t\t\t\t\t15276 text bananas \n\t\t\t\t\t15277 text or \n\t\t\t\t\t15278 text Dr. Pepper\n\t\t\t\t\t15279 text : \n\t\t\t\t\t15280 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15281 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15282 text • Dressing up bananas as former presidents can be considered art.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15283 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15284 text • Smearing banana onto a glass picture frame can be considered art.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15285 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15286 text • Letting a banana slowly dissolve in a glass of Dr. Pepper can be considered art.\n\t\t\t\t\t15287 text We know that Kenny would disagree with all these claims, since his restrictive wording allows us to apply his standard of "\n\t\t\t\t\t15288 text only\n\t\t\t\t\t15289 text  well-painted canvases" to an infinite number of novel scenarios. \n\t\t\t\t15290 image Problem / Solution - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15291 heading Problem / Solution - Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15292 text Problem / Solution - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15293 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t15294 text 1 hr, 7 mins\n\t\t\t\t15295 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15296 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15297 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15298 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15299 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15300 text Synopsis\n\t\t\t\t\t15301 text This is the 3rd most common RC framework, showing in about 17% of passages, especially Law and Science passages. Usually these passages end with the author providing some recommendation or corrective, so just like \n\t\t\t\t\t15302 text Answer a Question \n\t\t\t\t\t15303 text and \n\t\t\t\t\t15304 text Present Debate \n\t\t\t\t\t15305 text and \n\t\t\t\t\t15306 text Old / New, \n\t\t\t\t\t15307 text we often don\'t hear the Author\'s voice or main point until the final paragraph.\n\t\t\t\t\t15308 text But in some cases, the author never provides a solution, and so our main point ends up sounding like a description of the Problem. \n\t\t\t\t\t15309 text Identifying Features\n\t\t\t\t\t15310 text One of the interesting parts of Problem / Solution passages is that we\'re very likely to get the \n\t\t\t\t\t15311 text Main Point \n\t\t\t\t\t15312 text in the\n\t\t\t\t\t15313 text  final paragraph\n\t\t\t\t\t15314 text , because the author tends to spend two or three paragraphs acquainting us with a problematic situation.\n\t\t\t\t\t15315 text Some passages only describe a Problem. This is typical in Law passages, where an author might want to explore a thorny legal issue that doesn\'t have any clear answers right now.\n\t\t\t\t\t15316 text Some Humanities passages will feel like the author is simply complaining about something, without offering a better way. Similarly, we could think of these critique passages as Presenting a Problem, but never offering a solution.\n\t\t\t\t\t15317 text Sometimes, the author will present or evaluate \n\t\t\t\t\t15318 text other people\'s \n\t\t\t\t\t15319 text proposed Solutions. If the author implicitly agrees with someone else\'s solution, then she\'ll usually put it towards the end and offer no pushback. In other passages, though, the author will shoot down other people\'s potential solutions before proposing her own (or giving up that there is still no good solution).\n\t\t\t\t15320 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15321 text Get 4 out of your last 5 correct, \n\t\t\t\t\t15322 text to pass this Level.\n\t\t\t\t\t15323 text If it doesn\'t happen within 30 mins, that\'s fine. Feel free to keep working at it if you\'re so inclined, or to just come back to it at another time.\n\t\t\t\t\t15324 text As You\'re Reading ... \n\t\t\t\t\t15325 text \ufeffEarly Clues\n\t\t\t\t\t15326 text We are most likely to see hints of a problem in the first paragraph or usually by the first sentence of the 2nd paragraph at the latest. Words like "problematic", "the difficulty with this", "ambiguity", "uncertainty" and such suggest an air of tension.\n\t\t\t\t\t15327 text If we see an author pose a question or otherwise discuss smart people who have been trying to figure out how ____ , then answering that question is probably the central Problem the passage is focused on.\n\t\t\t\t\t15328 text Big Ideas to Track\n\t\t\t\t\t15329 text As you\'re reading these passages, look for language in the first paragraph or transition to the second that seems to be setting up something problematic or something negative.\n\t\t\t\t\t15330 text Start trying to fill in this blank: \n\t\t\t\t\t15331 text What is the \n\t\t\t\t\t15332 text Problem\n\t\t\t\t\t15333 text ? \n\t\t\t\t\t15334 text or otherwise, \n\t\t\t\t\t15335 text What \n\t\t\t\t\t15336 text Question \n\t\t\t\t\t15337 text are people trying to answer?\n\t\t\t\t\t15338 text As you learn more about it, keep reminding yourself of The Problem (or The Question). The other details don\'t matter, unless you can attach them to your strong, enduring memory of The Problem. Relate any details or new topics to the Problem.\n\t\t\t\t\t15339 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15340 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15341 text • Historical background  on the Problem?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15342 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15343 text • Causal explanation  for the Problem?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15344 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15345 text • Misconception  about the Problem?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15346 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15347 text • More  elaboration  on what the Problem is?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15348 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15349 text • Someone\'s opinion  about the Problem?\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15350 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15351 text • The  implications  if we don\'t solve this Problem?\n\t\t\t\t\t15352 text Will there be a Solution? Will there be a Recommendation? Omigosh, I\'m so excited, are you? I\'m obnoxiously overdramatizing to remind you to keep your ears open for hints that we\'re now pivoting into Solution territory. That\'s the other big idea we have to capture.\n\t\t\t\t\t15353 text If there\'s no Solution, then let\'s listen for a summary sentence towards the end in which the author wraps up the significance of the situation.\n\t\t\t\t15354 image Speedwalking LR (set 1)\n\t\t\t\t15355 heading Speedwalking LR (set 1), Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15356 text Speedwalking LR (set 1)\n\t\t\t\t15357 text Pacing\n\t\t\t\t15358 text 33 mins\n\t\t\t\t15359 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15360 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15361 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15362 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15363 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15364 text LENGTH\n\t\t\t\t\t15365 text  -- 15 Q\'s, 15 minutes (1.5x = 22, 2x = 30)\n\t\t\t\t\t15366 text TYPES\n\t\t\t\t\t15367 text  -- Paradox, Flaw, Role, Main Conclusion, Necessary Assumption, Sufficient Assumption, Strengthen, Weaken, Method, and Must Be True.\n\t\t\t\t\t15368 text LEVEL\n\t\t\t\t\t15369 text  -- 1\n\t\t\t\t\t15370 text Wait a sec -- these are all level 1? I thought this activity was listed as level 5?\n\t\t\t\t\t15371 text Yes, because the goal is something a level 5 student needs to work on:\xa0\xa0be able to quickly take care of easier questions, so that you\'ll have more time and brainpower in reserves for the harder, more flexible thinking questions in the section.\n\t\t\t\t\t15372 text \ufeffGiven how many subtle reading traps there are on LSAT, it\'s sometimes difficult to ever let yourself believe that an answer you find appealing is correct. "It\'s never this easy", we might think. But, sure it is! Sometimes it really is that easy. We need to improve our ability to \n\t\t\t\t\t15373 text let the easy be easy\n\t\t\t\t\t15374 text . \n\t\t\t\t\t15375 text And we need to develop enough self-trust while we\'re doing easier problems that we can pick up our pace when possible. \n\t\t\t\t15376 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15377 text Try to get through these 15 questions in 15 mins. Keep yourself going at a brisk pace. When you have a strong idea of what you\'re looking for (like on Main Conclusion, Role, Sufficient Assumption, Flaw), try to be proactive about scanning for and finding your answer, rather than reading all five choices start to finish.\n\t\t\t\t\t15378 text However, on tasks where we compare the impact of new information (like Paradox, Strengthen, Weaken), we may still need to use more time to consider all five answers.\n\t\t\t\t\t15379 text If your thinking feels unfinished on any of them, flag them as you go (so that you can maintain your brisk pace), and then take a second look at them after the timer goes off before you check your answer / the explanation.\n\t\t\t\t15380 image Science: Crop Crap\n\t\t\t\t15381 heading Science: Crop Crap, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15382 text Science: Crop Crap\n\t\t\t\t15383 text Pacing\n\t\t\t\t15384 text 33 mins\n\t\t\t\t15385 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15386 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15387 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15388 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15389 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15390 text As the inelegant name of this activity suggests, this is a pair of \n\t\t\t\t\t15391 text Science \n\t\t\t\t\t15392 text passages about  crops . \n\t\t\t\t\t15393 text You\'re welcome, you\'re welcome! Look, we had no choice. You guys have been blowing up our inbox requesting this. It feels good to finally deliver.\n\t\t\t\t\t15394 text You\'re doing this as a timed set.\xa0\xa0\n\t\t\t\t\t15395 text In other words, there\'s a small plot of land to harvest before the hurricane rolls in. You have 15-20 minutes. Grab the most get-able fruit while there\'s time! \n\t\t\t\t15396 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15397 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15398 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15399 text 1 . Set a timer for  18 minutes.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15400 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15401 text 2 . Attempt these two passages.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15402 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15403 text 3 . Select an answer to all 15 questions within the time limit, even if some of them are "flag-and-skip" answers.\n\t\t\t\t\t15404 text Once the timer goes off, and you go through answers / explanations, make sure you take 5 extra seconds as you\'re leaving each problem to mentally or vocally articulate a takeaway. Encode something in your subconscious: \n\t\t\t\t\t15405 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15406 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15407 text • something you did right\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15408 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15409 text • a question you wished you had asked yourself\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15410 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15411 text • a detail you wished you\'d noticed\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15412 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15413 text • a spot in the passage you wished you\'d researched\n\t\t\t\t15414 image Strengthen - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15415 heading Strengthen - Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15416 text Strengthen - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15417 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t15418 text 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t15419 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15420 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15421 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15422 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15423 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15424 text Get 4 out of your last 5 correct  to complete your \n\t\t\t\t\t15425 text Level\n\t\t\t\t\t15426 text  for \n\t\t\t\t\t15427 text level 5.\n\t\t\t\t15428 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15429 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15430 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15431 text • Set a timer for 20 minutes.\xa0If you haven\'t passed your level by the time the timer goes off, move on to something else or try another 10-15 mins if you want to keep pushing to clear the level.\n\t\t\t\t\t15432 text Try to articulate how your correct answer is helping the argument:\n\t\t\t\t\t15433 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15434 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15435 text • affirming  an  assumption ?\n\t\t\t\t\t15436 text (if the author was assuming "X is relevant to Y", a correct answer on strengthen might say something like "X is the most important factor for Y")\n\t\t\t\t\t15437 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15438 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15439 text • countering  a possible  objection  to the argument? \n\t\t\t\t\t15440 text (these answers are harder to interpret, if we didn\'t think of possible objections to the argument ahead of time. So even though this is \n\t\t\t\t\t15441 text Strengthen\n\t\t\t\t\t15442 text , don\'t neglect to figure out where the argument is vulnerable to criticism by considering objections, once you\'ve read the argument.\n\t\t\t\t\t15443 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15444 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15445 text • making the existing  evidence  seem  more compelling / relevant ?\n\t\t\t\t\t15446 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15447 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15448 text • adding  on some new consideration that gives \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15449 text yet another reason\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15450 text  to believe the Conclusion?\n\t\t\t\t15451 image PrepTest 141 - Section 1\n\t\t\t\t15452 heading PrepTest 141 - Section 1, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15453 text PrepTest 141 - Section 1\n\t\t\t\t15454 text Timed Section 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t15455 button Take Section\n\t\t\t\t\t15456 text Take Section\n\t\t\t\t15457 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15458 image PrepTest 142 - Section 4\n\t\t\t\t15459 heading PrepTest 142 - Section 4, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15460 text PrepTest 142 - Section 4\n\t\t\t\t15461 text Timed Section 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t15462 button Take Section\n\t\t\t\t\t15463 text Take Section\n\t\t\t\t15464 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15465 image PrepTest 155\n\t\t\t\t15466 heading PrepTest 155, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15467 text PrepTest 155\n\t\t\t\t15468 text Practice Test 4 hrs, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t15469 button Take Test\n\t\t\t\t\t15470 text Take Test\n\t\t\t\t15471 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15472 button \uf2c2\n\t\t\t\t\t15473 text \uf2c2\n\t\t\t15474 container\n\t\t\t\t15475 heading Week 14, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t15476 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15477 text Week  14\n\t\t\t\t15478 text December 27th, 2026 - January 2nd, 2027\n\t\t\t\t15479 text Est. Time Remaining:  22 hrs, 7 mins\n\t\t\t\t15480 text \uf113\n\t\t\t\t15481 image Science - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15482 heading Science - Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15483 text Science - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15484 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t15485 text 1 hr, 7 mins\n\t\t\t\t15486 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15487 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15488 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15489 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15490 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15491 heading Common Frameworks, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15492 text Common Frameworks\n\t\t\t\t\t15493 text The most common frameworks in Science passages are \n\t\t\t\t\t15494 text Old/New, Problem/Solution \n\t\t\t\t\t15495 text and \n\t\t\t\t\t15496 text Present a Debate\n\t\t\t\t\t15497 text . There is significant overlap here, as Old/New will frequently be applicable (there was an Old question we couldn\'t answer, but \n\t\t\t\t\t15498 text recent\n\t\t\t\t\t15499 text  findings suggest a New possible answer or solution, or there was a traditional school of thought and now there is a new school of thought coming at the same topic from a different point of view).\n\t\t\t\t15500 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15501 text Get 4 out of your last 5 correct, \n\t\t\t\t\t15502 text to pass this Level.\n\t\t\t\t\t15503 text If it doesn\'t happen within 30 mins, that\'s fine. Feel free to keep working at it if you\'re so inclined, or to just come back to it at another time.\n\t\t\t\t\t15504 text As You\'re Reading\n\t\t\t\t\t15505 text If the details feel overwhelming, stop reading for a sec, and just remind yourself of the Big Ideas from your framework.\n\t\t\t\t\t15506 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15507 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15508 text • What is the question / problem  that scientists have been asking or trying to solve?\n\t\t\t\t\t15509 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15510 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15511 text • What is the answer / solution  to that question or problem?\n\t\t\t\t\t15512 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15513 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15514 text • This debate is about what  topic, mystery, phenomenon, or question?\n\t\t\t\t\t15515 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15516 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15517 text • What is the difference  between Point of View 1 and Point of View 2 (or 3 or 4). Define it in an oppositional "they believe X / they believe not-X" or "fast growth vs. slow growth" kind of way. Don\'t just say words associated with each side of the debate; make sure you frame them as logical opposites in some way.\n\t\t\t\t\t15518 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15519 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15520 text • Does the Author show up at the end  to let us know how she feels about this Debate or how she feels about this New answer/solution we\'re considering?\n\t\t\t\t\t15521 text Optional "Deluxe" Practice\n\t\t\t\t\t15522 text Pop open the NOTES panel (bottom left of the screen has a little page icon) and move/resize the NOTES window so that it covers the answers. Don\'t look at the answers until you\'ve \n\t\t\t\t\t15523 text written your prediction\n\t\t\t\t\t15524 text .\n\t\t\t\t\t15525 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15526 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15527 text • sometimes our prediction comes from our gut understanding\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15528 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15529 text • sometimes our prediction is simply "last sentence of paragraph 3"\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15530 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15531 text • sometimes you can\'t make a prediction (you can write "no prediction")\n\t\t\t\t\t15532 text When you ultimately see the correct answer, you can assess how well-aligned your prediction was / wasn\'t, and potentially learn more about that stage of the process.\n\t\t\t\t\t15533 text When you go to start looking at the answers, move the notes panel to the side and \n\t\t\t\t\t15534 text write in why you\'re rejecting each wrong answer\n\t\t\t\t\t15535 text . When you ultimately see the explanation, you can compare your reason to ours and see if there\'s anything to refine about your thinking there. \n\t\t\t\t15536 image Assumption Family (Harder) Set 2\n\t\t\t\t15537 heading Assumption Family (Harder) Set 2, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15538 text Assumption Family (Harder) Set 2\n\t\t\t\t15539 text Pacing\n\t\t\t\t15540 text 1 hr\n\t\t\t\t15541 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15542 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15543 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15544 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15545 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15546 text This is a \n\t\t\t\t\t15547 text tough \n\t\t\t\t\t15548 text timed set of Assumption Family problems from test 72, all level 4 or 5.
