Before timer runs out,  get an answer to all 10  problems, so that you can practice the tough habit of moving on even though you weren\'t fully done thinking about the problem.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15577 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15578 text 3 . Once the timer goes off,  take an untimed 2nd look  at problems before you check your previous attempt and look at the explanation.\n\t\t\t\t\t15579 text Don\'t do this activity as your first LSAT activity of the day. It would be like not stretching at all and then just jumping into the 4th quarter of an NBA playoff game. Get your brain ready to have a really powerful stretch of high-processing efficiency for 20 mins. \n\t\t\t\t15580 image Principle-Strengthen - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15581 heading Principle-Strengthen - Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15582 text Principle-Strengthen - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15583 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t15584 text 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t15585 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15586 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15587 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15588 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15589 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15590 text Get 4 out of your last 5 correct\n\t\t\t\t\t15591 text , to pass this Level.\n\t\t\t\t\t15592 text question stem keywords\n\t\t\t\t\t15593 text principle, if valid / if assumed / if established, most justifies, most supports\n\t\t\t\t\t15594 text examples\n\t\t\t\t\t15595 text Which principle, if valid, most justifies the reasoning in the argument? Which principle, if established, most helps to justify the decision?\n\t\t\t\t15596 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15597 heading Principle-Strengthen, Value: 4\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15598 text Principle-Strengthen\n\t\t\t\t\t15599 heading   , Value: 4\n\t\t\t\t\t15600 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15601 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15602 text • Find the CONCLUSION and the EVIDENCE.\n\t\t\t\t\t15603 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15604 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15605 text • Pre-phrase "IF premise, THEN conclusion".\n\t\t\t\t\t15606 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15607 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15608 text • The correct answer should sound like 1/2 Premise language, 1/2 Conclusion language.\n\t\t\t\t\t15609 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15610 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15611 text • Try to get rid of answer choices quickly if they don\'t have Conclusion language\n\t\t\t\t\t15612 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15613 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15614 text • Also be wary of answers that put the Conclusion on the  left  side of arrow, or that say "not the Conclusion" on the  right  of the arrow.\n\t\t\t\t\t15615 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15616 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15617 text • If there are competing interests being weighted against each other, the correct answer may rank one thing as more important than another. We call this style of answer " weighing tradeoffs ".\n\t\t\t\t15618 image Society - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15619 heading Society - Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15620 text Society - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15621 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t15622 text 1 hr, 7 mins\n\t\t\t\t15623 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15624 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15625 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15626 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15627 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15628 heading Common Frameworks, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15629 text Common Frameworks\n\t\t\t\t\t15630 text Society is harder to pin down. Topics in economics, sociology, and psychology tend to be more \n\t\t\t\t\t15631 text Challenge Position\n\t\t\t\t\t15632 text  (clarifying a misconception, usually) or \n\t\t\t\t\t15633 text Present Debate\n\t\t\t\t\t15634 text . Meanwhile, the passages that feel more like hard sciences about past cultures are more likely to have an \n\t\t\t\t\t15635 text Old / New \n\t\t\t\t\t15636 text or \n\t\t\t\t\t15637 text Problem / Solution \n\t\t\t\t\t15638 text vibe. But you also see a fair number of \n\t\t\t\t\t15639 text Theme / Example \n\t\t\t\t\t15640 text and \n\t\t\t\t\t15641 text Highlight Noteworthy\n\t\t\t\t\t15642 text  passages.\n\t\t\t\t\t15643 heading   , Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t15644 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15645 text Get 4 out of your last 5 correct, \n\t\t\t\t\t15646 text to pass this Level.\n\t\t\t\t\t15647 text If it doesn\'t happen within 30 mins, that\'s fine. Feel free to keep working at it if you\'re so inclined, or to just come back to it at another time.\n\t\t\t\t\t15648 text Big Picture Reading Practice\n\t\t\t\t\t15649 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15650 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15651 text • See if there\'s any foreshadowing in that first paragraph, that\'s either setting up a  Position  (most studies have concluded, many people think), setting up a  Problem  (possibly asking a question like, "When did humans first start riding horses?), setting up a  Generalization  (something broad followed by  for example  or  a case in point ), or a  Debate  (proponents / opponents, some X\'s say / other X\'s say)\n\t\t\t\t\t15652 text As you read, keep testing yourself on retention by looking away from the screen and seeing if you can comfortably say the Main Ideas in your own words.\n\t\t\t\t\t15653 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15654 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15655 text • The question they\'re trying to answer is...\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15656 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15657 text • The reason we care about this book / this study / this person / this movement / this situation is because...\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15658 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15659 text • Side A of the debate believes... / Side B of the debate believes...\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15660 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15661 text • The Old idea was... / The New idea is...\n\t\t\t\t\t15662 text (Optional) Deluxe Learning Mode\n\t\t\t\t\t15663 text This takes longer, but makes a bigger difference on our brains. Use the NOTES panel (the page icon in the bottom left of the page pops open a NOTES panel you can move around) to record your thoughts. \n\t\t\t\t\t15664 text Big Picture Retention\n\t\t\t\t\t15665 text When you\'re done reading the passage, cover up the passage and type in your memory of the big ideas. If you\'re finding that you \n\t\t\t\t\t15666 text thought \n\t\t\t\t\t15667 text you understood what you were reading, but it\'s very hard to remember what to write down once you\'re not looking at the passage anymore, that means that you\'re not doing enough \n\t\t\t\t\t15668 text self-summarizing \n\t\t\t\t\t15669 text yet. When we read big ideas, we pause on those sentences long enough to digest them and simplify them in our own personal wording. This process is what leads to strong retention. We have an easier time remembering our own words than remembering an LSAT author\'s.\n\t\t\t\t\t15670 text Pre-phrasing\n\t\t\t\t\t15671 text When you\'re ready to start working through actual questions, use the NOTES panel to cover up the answer choices. Read a question stem, do whatever research you need to in the passage, and then type into the NOTES panel what you think the correct answer should say, or which sentence(s) will be the supporting text for the correct answer. If the question stem has no keywords, feel free to write nothing, or "no pre-phrase", or "beware strong language on first pass".\n\t\t\t\t\t15672 text Answer Evaluation \n\t\t\t\t\t15673 text Resize the NOTES panel so that you can see answers again, and when you pick your answer, type into the NOTES panel where your supporting text was found (you might need more than one sentence to support your answer, but usually it\'s just one sentence). Also type into the NOTES panel a specific reason why you\'re eliminating each answer choice. Don\'t just say "Out of Scope" without indicating which word or idea is out of scope. Don\'t just say "Too Strong" without typing which word or phrase was too strong. If everything in an answer is accurate, then list some other reason like Too Narrow for why it\'s wrong.\n\t\t\t\t15674 image Conditional Logic (Harder) Set 3\n\t\t\t\t15675 heading Conditional Logic (Harder) Set 3, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15676 text Conditional Logic (Harder) Set 3\n\t\t\t\t15677 text Pacing\n\t\t\t\t15678 text 37 mins\n\t\t\t\t15679 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15680 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15681 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15682 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15683 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15684 text Focus on finding \n\t\t\t\t\t15685 text Conditional Indicator\n\t\t\t\t\t15686 text  words and using them as a way to organize how you write or think about the If / Then rule. Write or think through the contrapositive as well. Beware the temptation to make illegal Backwards or Opposite moves.\n\t\t\t\t\t15687 text Conditional Logic intersects with different question types differently:\n\t\t\t\t\t15688 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15689 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15690 text • Principle  (the left side of the Principle matches the Evidence, the right side matches the Conclusion)\n\t\t\t\t\t15691 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15692 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15693 text • Parallel (diagramming these arguments with "algebraic recipes" allows us to be more picky and decisive when evaluating answers)\n\t\t\t\t\t15694 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15695 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15696 text • Assumption (the conclusion gives us an A --> Z logic path we want to prove, and the evidence + the correct answer choice assemble together to create that A --> Z path\xa0\xa0/ or the evidence gives us a conditional rule that is being used in drawing the conclusion, but we still need an answer choice to tell us something in order to clearly trigger that rule.)\n\t\t\t\t\t15697 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15698 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15699 text • Must Be True / Most Supported (multiple conditionals often chain together, and provided facts often match the contrapositive-trigger of a conditional and allow us to infer the contrapositive-outcome)\n\t\t\t\t\t15700 text \ufeff\n\t\t\t\t\t15701 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15702 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15703 text • Flaw / Parallel Flaw (Flaw + Conditional Logic usually means the  Necessary vs. Sufficient  flaw, which is using a rule in an illegal Backwards or Opposite fashion. Sometimes it involves messing up Or / And stuff)\n\t\t\t\t15704 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15705 text Try these 6 questions, \n\t\t\t\t\t15706 text level 5.\n\t\t\t\t\t15707 text Try them all within \n\t\t\t\t\t15708 text 11 minutes\n\t\t\t\t\t15709 text  (or 16, or 22), then circle back and confirm your thinking (untimed) before checking your previous answer and looking at the explanation.\n\t\t\t\t\t15710 text CONDITIONAL KEYWORDS\n\t\t\t\t\t15711 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15712 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15713 text • Put on  LEFT \n\t\t\t\t\t15714 text \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0if\n\t\t\t\t\t15715 text , when, any, each, all, every, the only, whenever, whoever, X\'s \n\t\t\t\t\t15716 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15717 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15718 text • Put it on the  RIGHT\n\t\t\t\t\t15719 text \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0only if\n\t\t\t\t\t15720 text , only, must, requires, ensures, will, always, implies, \n\t\t\t\t\t15721 text \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0presupposes, depends on, guarantees, \n\t\t\t\t\t15722 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15723 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15724 text • Put negated version of either idea on left ( IF-NOT )\n\t\t\t\t\t15725 text \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0unless\n\t\t\t\t\t15726 text , without, until except\n\t\t\t\t\t15727 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15728 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15729 text • NEGATIVE  to Positive conversions\n\t\t\t\t\t15730 text \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0No \n\t\t\t\t\t15731 text A\'s are B = All A\'s are ~B \n\t\t\t\t\t15732 text \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Not all A\'s are B = Some A\'s are ~B\n\t\t\t\t\t15733 text \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Few A\'s are B = Most A\'s are ~B\n\t\t\t\t15734 image Parallel - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15735 heading Parallel - Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15736 text Parallel - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15737 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t15738 text 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t15739 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15740 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15741 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15742 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15743 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15744 heading FINAL SHOWDOWN, Value: 1\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15745 text FINAL SHOWDOWN\n\t\t\t\t\t15746 heading 1\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15747 image\n\t\t\t\t\t15748 heading Level 5, Value: 1\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15749 text Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15750 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15751 text Get 4 of your last 5 correct\n\t\t\t\t\t15752 text ,  to clear this Level.\n\t\t\t\t15753 image Present Debate - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15754 heading Present Debate - Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15755 text Present Debate - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15756 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t15757 text 1 hr, 7 mins\n\t\t\t\t15758 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15759 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15760 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15761 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15762 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15763 text Synopsis\n\t\t\t\t\t15764 text Present a Debate is a common framework on Society and Law passages. After all, scholars in soft sciences (economics / anthropology / sociology, etc.) and legal scholars end up having to debate all the time because their subject matter is so frequently nuanced and many shades of gray.\xa0\n\t\t\t\t\t15765 text About 15% of passages are tagged with this framework. Usually the author inserts her opinion at the end of the passage, so these are commonly "Late-Thesis" type passages. Sometimes, though, the author stays out and just literally \n\t\t\t\t\t15766 text presents \n\t\t\t\t\t15767 text the debate without editorializing. \n\t\t\t\t\t15768 text Once you start to see 2 non-author points of view, think about what central question they\'re both addressing or answering. As you try to encode the main idea of each side of the debate, try to use \n\t\t\t\t\t15769 text Oppositional Pairings \n\t\t\t\t\t15770 text if possible.\n\t\t\t\t\t15771 text It\'s harder to remember, "Side A is in favor of more stringent COVID mitigation precautions" whereas "Side B thinks that the accompanying harms of remote learning and shuttered small businesses outweigh the health risks of staying open".\n\t\t\t\t\t15772 text It\'s easier to remember, "Side A is in favor of more lockdowns for a while, Side B opposes more lockdowns". So try to boil down each side\'s position into similar wording. Even if it\'s not binary "A vs. not-A" wording, we can make it fill in a common blank like, "Side A thinks the dinosaurs were killed by climate change, Side B says respiratory disease".\n\t\t\t\t15773 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15774 text Get 4 out of your last 5 correct, \n\t\t\t\t\t15775 text to pass this Level.\n\t\t\t\t\t15776 text If it doesn\'t happen within 30 mins, that\'s fine. Feel free to keep working at it if you\'re so inclined, or to just come back to it at another time.\n\t\t\t\t\t15777 text As You\'re Reading ... \n\t\t\t\t\t15778 text \ufeffEarly Clues\n\t\t\t\t\t15779 text We see at least two points of view (POVs) that are not the author. We might see early attributions like, "Some critics say X. Others say Y", or perhaps we\'ll see mention of both Opponents and Proponents. Or there will be two schools of thought named (steady-state economists believe X, but neoclassical believe Y).\n\t\t\t\t\t15780 text Big Ideas to Track\n\t\t\t\t\t15781 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15782 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15783 text 1 . The central question being debated\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15784 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15785 text 2 . Side A\xa0\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15786 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15787 text 3 . Side B\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15788 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15789 text 4 . The Author\'s Take (if any)\xa0\n\t\t\t\t\t15790 text Common Variations\n\t\t\t\t\t15791 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15792 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15793 text • The author picks a winner\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15794 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15795 text • The author offers a 3rd option\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15796 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15797 text • The author agrees with both, somewhat, but neither overall\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15798 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15799 text • The author never makes her position known (in which case the main point becomes that "there is a debate")\n\t\t\t\t15800 image with illegal reversals or negations.\n\t\t\t\t15840 image Parallel Flaw - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15841 heading Parallel Flaw - Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15842 text Parallel Flaw - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15843 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15850 heading The Final Showdown, Value: 1\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15851 text The Final Showdown\n\t\t\t\t\t15852 heading 1\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15853 image\n\t\t\t\t\t15854 heading Level 5, Value: 1\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15855 text Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15856 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15857 text Get 4 out of 5 correct,\n\t\t\t\t\t15858 text to pass this Level.\n\t\t\t\t15859 image Principle-Conform: Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15860 heading Principle-Conform: Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15861 text Principle-Conform: Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15862 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t15863 text 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t15864 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15865 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15866 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15867 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15868 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15869 text There are three varieties of \n\t\t\t\t\t15870 text Principle-Conform\n\t\t\t\t\t15871 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15872 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15873 text • The stimulus is a principle (or pair of principles)\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15874 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15875 text • The answers are principles\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15876 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15877 text • There are no explicit principles, just implied/illustrated ones\n\t\t\t\t\t15878 text Principles in Stimulus\n\t\t\t\t\t15879 text When the stimulus is providing an explicit principle (or two), we\'re usually being tested on our ability to apply a conditional rule. \n\t\t\t\t\t15880 text To find an answer that Conforms to this principle, we want an answer where the situation described matches the Trigger of the principle, and the judgment concluded matches the Outcome of the principle. (Even when the principles aren\'t expressed as conditionals, there will still usually be two things we need to make sure match up).\n\t\t\t\t\t15881 text Principles in Answers\n\t\t\t\t\t15882 text It\'s essentially the same mindset as a Principle-Strengthen question. We read the argument and then anticipate the principle underlying the argument by pre-phrasing "IF evidence, THEN conclusion". We expect the correct answer to \n\t\t\t\t\t15883 text Link \n\t\t\t\t\t15884 text language from the Evidence to the Conclusion\'s language.\xa0All that\'s different is that because the question stem says \n\t\t\t\t\t15885 text conform \n\t\t\t\t\t15886 text to the author\'s reasoning, we can\'t pick an answer that\'s overly strong. (That usually doesn\'t matter, but occasionally it does)\n\t\t\t\t\t15887 text Implicit Principles\n\t\t\t\t\t15888 text These feel similar to Parallel reasoning questions, because we\'re given an argument in the stimulus, and then each answer choice is its own argument on its own unique topic. We\'re looking for an underlying similarity to connect the correct answer to the original argument.\n\t\t\t\t\t15889 text On Parallel questions, those similarities come more in the form of technical / structural similarities (i.e. "Since the original argument had a \n\t\t\t\t\t15890 text Most \n\t\t\t\t\t15891 text premise and a \n\t\t\t\t\t15892 text Some \n\t\t\t\t\t15893 text premise, the correct answer\'s argument will also have those features").\n\t\t\t\t\t15894 text But with Principle-Conform it\'s more about the underlying gist or rule-of-thumb. We don\'t try to diagram the arguments. We just want to articulate a general moral to the story or operating principle that\'s guiding the author\'s thinking, and then we try to find an answer that matches that.\n\t\t\t\t15895 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15896 text Get 4 of your last 5 correct, \n\t\t\t\t\t15897 text untimed\n\t\t\t\t\t15898 text , to pass this \n\t\t\t\t\t15899 text level\n\t\t\t\t\t15900 text .\n\t\t\t\t15901 image Speed Drill - Level 2\n\t\t\t\t15902 heading Speed Drill - Level 2, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15903 text Speed Drill - Level 2\n\t\t\t\t15904 text Pacing\n\t\t\t\t15905 text 45 mins\n\t\t\t\t15906 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15907 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15908 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15909 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15910 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15911 text This is a trio of \n\t\t\t\t\t15912 text level 2\n\t\t\t\t\t15913 text  passages from tests 62, 64, 69. There\'s a \n\t\t\t\t\t15914 text Present Debate\n\t\t\t\t\t15915 text , an \n\t\t\t\t\t15916 text Old / New\n\t\t\t\t\t15917 text , and a \n\t\t\t\t\t15918 text Problem / Solution\n\t\t\t\t\t15919 text  passage, although you could probably see all three as Problem / Solution, if you prefer.\n\t\t\t\t\t15920 text The goal of this exercise is to practice a sustained, brisk "speedwalking" pace. When the test is offering us its easier items, we need to act like it.\n\t\t\t\t\t15921 text We need to try pushing our pace so that we can bank some extra time to spend on the hardest parts of a section.\n\t\t\t\t15922 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15923 text Set yourself an appropriate time limit.\n\t\t\t\t\t15924 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15925 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15926 text • If you aren\'t yet used to finishing all four passages with enough time, give yourself  27  mins for this threesome. \n\t\t\t\t\t15927 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15928 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15929 text • If you tend to get through all four, then try doing them in  22  mins. \n\t\t\t\t\t15930 text Either way, keep your eye on the clock and have a guess for all 21 Q\'s (even if it\'s a blind guess). \n\t\t\t\t\t15931 text The time limit is supposed to force us into experimenting with new behaviors:\n\t\t\t\t\t15932 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15933 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15934 text • when you have high confidence about an answer choice, pick it and move on without worrying about reading all the other answers you haven\'t seen yet. (high confidence comes when we find an answer choice that matches the  meaning  of a line in the passage, but an exact  language  match usually means a trap answer. but  doesn\'t  match up with language in the passage, but we can tell LSAT has put some work into disguising it with synonyms or different syntax. \n\t\t\t\t\t15935 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15936 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15937 text • if you get four or five words into an answer choice and already see something you don\'t like, get out of there. we need to conserve time and mental energy by not processing the full sentence of every answer choice. find  earlier  reasons to disqualify an answer.\n\t\t\t\t\t15938 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15939 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15940 text • get the passage read in 2.5 minutes or less. be content to simply determine the topic and framework, find the ideas that fill your framework boxes, and don\'t worry about grabbing too much else. Read the first paragraph carefully, and read the 1st sentence of other paragraphs carefully, and read any  pivot  sentences ( but, yet, however ) carefully. Let the rest of it breeze by.\n\t\t\t\t\t15941 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15942 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15943 text • skip the worst problem in each passage set. we will tend to overspend time on that even though we have a lower average accuracy on that problem, so it\'s a bad value.\n\t\t\t\t\t15944 text Hit SUBMIT SET when the timer runs out. Then take a 2nd untimed look at the questions and explanations.\n\t\t\t\t15945 image Role - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15946 heading Role - Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15947 text Role - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t15948 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t15949 text 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t15950 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15951 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15952 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15953 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15954 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15955 text On harder \n\t\t\t\t\t15956 text Role \n\t\t\t\t\t15957 text questions, we\'re likely to see a couple patterns emerge:\n\t\t\t\t\t15958 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15959 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15960 text • Intermediate Conclusion?  Many of the harder problems test the existence of an Intermediate Conclusion, even if the claim we\'re being asked about isn\'t itself that. Answer choices describing a Premise might differ by saying, "It\'s provides direct support for the Conclusion" vs. "It provide support for a claim that then provides direct support for the Conclusion".\n\t\t\t\t\t15961 text To assess whether a claim is or isn\'t an Intermediate Conclusion, we want to ask ourselves, "\n\t\t\t\t\t15962 text Is there\n\t\t\t\t\t15963 text Support\n\t\t\t\t\t15964 text  for this claim? Why should we believe this claim? Does anything else in the paragraph sound like it\'s answering that question?"\n\t\t\t\t\t15965 text Often, when there \n\t\t\t\t\t15966 text isn\'t \n\t\t\t\t\t15967 text a supporting idea present and thus the claim you\'re examining is really just a Premise, it\'s useful to think about how \n\t\t\t\t\t15968 text you\n\t\t\t\t\t15969 text would support that claim.\n\t\t\t\t\t15970 text If you\'re asking yourself, "Was the claim \n\t\t\t\t\t15971 text You shouldn\'t tell jokes at a funeral \n\t\t\t\t\t15972 text supported?" Supply your own answer, just get your brain hearing what actual support would sound like:\xa0\xa0"you shouldn\'t tell jokes at a funeral \n\t\t\t\t\t15973 text because\n\t\t\t\t\t15974 text ... funerals are a somber occasion and telling jokes makes it seem like you\'re not respecting the gravity of the situation". By articulating what support would sound like, you can sometimes help strengthen your conviction that no support was provided, if you\'re not seeing any claims like that.\n\t\t\t\t\t15975 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t15976 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t15977 text • Relational language, rather than classic Argument Role language.  Harder problems tend to supply fewer answers with recognizable terms like "Premise, Conclusion, Intermediate Conclusion" and either use more complicated abstract phrases to signify the same idea, or they don\'t really concern themselves with those labels at all. Instead, they just conversationally describe how the claims relate to each other, almost more like a  Method  of reasoning question. \n\t\t\t\t15978 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15979 text Get 4 out of your last 5 correct,\n\t\t\t\t\t15980 text to pass this level.\n\t\t\t\t15981 image Speedwalking LR (set 2)\n\t\t\t\t15982 heading Speedwalking LR (set 2), Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t15983 text Speedwalking LR (set 2)\n\t\t\t\t15984 text Pacing\n\t\t\t\t15985 text 45 mins\n\t\t\t\t15986 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t15987 text Info\n\t\t\t\t15988 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t15989 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t15990 container\n\t\t\t\t\t15991 text LENGTH\n\t\t\t\t\t15992 text  -- 15 Q\'s, 15 minutes (1.5x = 22, 2x = 30)\n\t\t\t\t\t15993 text TYPES\n\t\t\t\t\t15994 text  -- Paradox, Flaw, Role, Main Conclusion, Necessary Assumption, Sufficient Assumption, Strengthen, Weaken, Method, and Must Be True.\n\t\t\t\t\t15995 text LEVEL\n\t\t\t\t\t15996 text  -- 1\n\t\t\t\t\t15997 text Wait a sec -- these are all level 1? I thought this activity was listed as level 5?\n\t\t\t\t\t15998 text Yes, because the goal is something a level 5 student needs to work on:\xa0\xa0be able to quickly take care of easier questions, so that you\'ll have more time and brainpower in reserves for the harder, more flexible thinking questions in the section.\n\t\t\t\t\t15999 text Given how many subtle reading traps there are on LSAT, it\'s sometimes difficult to ever let yourself believe that an answer you find appealing is correct. "It\'s never this easy", we might think. But, sure it is! Sometimes it really is that easy. We need to improve our ability to \n\t\t\t\t\t16000 text let the easy be easy\n\t\t\t\t\t16001 text .\n\t\t\t\t\t16002 text And we need to develop enough self-trust while we\'re doing easier problems that we can pick up our pace when possible.\n\t\t\t\t16003 container\n\t\t\t\t\t16004 text Try to get through these 15 questions in 15 mins. Keep yourself going at a brisk pace. When you have a strong idea of what you\'re looking for (like on Main Conclusion, Role, Sufficient Assumption, Flaw), try to be proactive about scanning for and finding your answer, rather than reading all five choices start to finish.\n\t\t\t\t\t16005 text However, on tasks where we compare the impact of new information (like Paradox, Strengthen, Weaken), we may still need to use more time to consider all five answers.\n\t\t\t\t\t16006 text If your thinking feels unfinished on any of them, flag them as you go (so that you can maintain your brisk pace), and then take a second look at them after the timer goes off before you check your answer / the explanation.\n\t\t\t\t16007 image PrepTest 141 - Section 3\n\t\t\t\t16008 heading PrepTest 141 - Section 3, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t16009 text PrepTest 141 - Section 3\n\t\t\t\t16010 text Timed Section 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t16011 button Take Section\n\t\t\t\t\t16012 text Take Section\n\t\t\t\t16013 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t16014 image PrepTest 143 - Section 1\n\t\t\t\t16015 heading PrepTest 143 - Section 1, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t16016 text PrepTest 143 - Section 1\n\t\t\t\t16017 text Timed Section 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t16018 button Take Section\n\t\t\t\t\t16019 text Take Section\n\t\t\t\t16020 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t16021 image PrepTest 156\n\t\t\t\t16022 heading PrepTest 156, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t16023 text PrepTest 156\n\t\t\t\t16024 text Practice Test 4 hrs, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t16025 button Take Test\n\t\t\t\t\t16026 text Take Test\n\t\t\t\t16027 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t16028 button \uf2c2\n\t\t\t\t\t16029 text \uf2c2\n\t\t\t16030 container\n\t\t\t\t16031 heading Week 15, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t16032 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t16033 text Week  15\n\t\t\t\t16034 text January 3rd - 9th, 2027\n\t\t\t\t16035 text Est. Am I willing to try doing this? When is my next opportunity that I can try doing this?"\n  },\n  {\n    position: 16,\n    title: \'Find a Framework\',\n    text: "This 30 minute animated lesson introduces the Top 5 Frameworks for RC passages. Frameworks are kind of like movie / literary genres. Within a genre or framework, you can have some reliable guesses about what the big moments will be and when they\'ll come.\\n" +\n      `This video won\'t do much to change your brain unless you resolve to follow up on watching it by trying it on a couple passages. \ufeffSo pay attention to what you\'re watching with the thought of, "Right after I watch this, I\'m spending 5-10 minutes reading some first paragraphs from some random RC passages and attempting to pick a framework."`\n  },\n  {\n    position: 17,\n    title: \'Finding Frameworks (round 1)\',\n    text: "Reading the first paragraph, we want to feel like detectives. We\'re taking in the meaning of the early sentences, but we\'re trying to solve a mystery:What is the central topic? Why is the author writing about it? Which of the big 5 (CHOPP) or 7 total frameworks (CHOPPIE) could we use to organize the big ideas in this passage?\\n" +\n      "With each card, read the first paragraph and think about which framework(s) would seem usable. If there are multiple paragraphs, feel free to update your choice of Framework if the passage goes somewhere you weren\'t predicting.Set a 10 minute timer. \ufeffWhen it\'s goes off, you\'re good to go, unless you\'re feeling like doing more. "\n  },\n  {\n    position: 39,\n    title: "Challenge Position - Author\'s Intent",\n    text: "From three Challenge Position passages from tests 37, 40, and 52, this set has nine questions that test our understanding of the author\'s meaning and intent. Author\'s AttitudeLocal PurposeMeaning in ContextParagraph Purpose\\n" +\n      `Attempt the problems untimed. You\'ve probably read these passage before, so do what you gotta do to remind yourself of their contents. On Attitude, beware strong answers. Find at least one attitudinal marker in the passage to support your answer. On Local Purpose questions (in order to / serves to / primarily to), expect the correct answer to sound a lot like language from the previous sentence. The correct answer is all about the local Big Idea that this specific detail is supporting. On Meaning In Context, try to think of your own word or phrase that would fit into the same blank (and test answers by substituting them into place in the passage). If it\'s asking what a word/phrase refers to, then it\'s really testing us on understanding how the author was using some word/phrase in order to callback to some earlier detail, so we just want to track down that earlier moment.On Paragraph Purpose, pay close attention to the first sentence of the paragraph (unless they\'re asking about the very first paragraph). So, respectively, we end up looking for missing ideas or connections in the body of evidence presented, or we try to think about what types of issues haven\'t even been considered so far. Most answers can be lumped into one of these two buckets.those testing the Internal Logic of the argument ("in the box" ideas) those testing New Considerations ("outside the box" ideas)This set of problems is all about the Internal Logic, the missing facts or missing links in the argument. Usually the argument missing a connection between certain language in the evidence and certain language in the conclusion, but sometimes it\'s missing a connection between the language in two premises. \\n` +\n      "Try these six questions, untimed.Find the Conclusion. Find the main Supporting Idea (the Premise).On Assumption questions, try to find an answer reinforcing If Premise, then ConclusionIf you\'re doing Strengthen, look for answers sayingThe Premise is heavily connected to the ConclusionIf it\'s Flaw or Weaken, look for answers sayingThe Premise can be true, while the Conclusion is false"\n  },\n  {\n    position: 56,\n    title: \'Strength of Language\',\n    text: "Spend about 5-10 minutes on this Flashcard set, with the goal of making your brain focus on the strength of language in each answer choice. Take the idea of "correct" answers with a grain of salt. This is somewhat subjective and open to different takes. We\'re mainly trying to get our brains to care more about this.Strong wording will be stuff like only, unless, requires, must, cannot, always,\xa0\xa0best, most important. These answers aren\'t automatically wrong, but we shouldn\'t feel comfortable picking them unless we\'ve found unequivocal supporting language. Mid-grade stuff will include the Most family (most, typically, usually, generally, tends to, rarely, few) and answers making Comparative claims. If a comparison is speaking to a really broad set of things, e.g. "men are better at golf than women", it\'s got a really high burden of proof. You\'d have to know a ton of data points about men and women and their golfing ability.The safe language will be stuff that can be proven true with only one data point: can, may, might, some, sometimes, need not, not all, not always.Build a better sensitivity to these words, but don\'t reduce the whole thing to individual words. Since he did manage to spare her the mockery, he was justified in lying.In order to use this Rule to prove that a lie was justified, we have to establish the trigger:the lie did more good than harmSo the correct answer would need to convince us that "keeping Sharon from getting mocked = did more good than harm".(Note: there are two styles of Principle-Strengthen question:\xa0\xa0Principles in Stimulus vs. Principle in Answers. The latter kind is more than 10x more common, but the former kind shows up more on modern tests than it used to)\\n` +\n      "Think about each Principle as having some criteria that must be met to trigger the rule, and having an outcome that matches up with the Application\'s conclusion. It\'s also one of the most fun, because it basically wants us to think like Opposing Counsel, hearing an LSAT author make her case and then responding, "Objection ... that argument is faulty because, [answer choice]."It\'s also one of the complex question types, because the answers come in different styles:an Assumption the author supposedly madean overlooked idea that would supposedly be an Objectionan abstract description of an Illegal Move the author supposedly made\\n` +\n      `Watch the lesson on Flaw questions.At its simplest, Flaw just wants us to read someone\'s unsuccessful argument and say to the judge, "Objection, Your Honor, but Stupid McDumbface just did _____ ."Thus, try to read the argument and respond with an objection to the reasoning. Is there a distinction the author isn\'t perceiving? Is the author\'s conclusion too strong? Is something irrelevant? Does the author\'s thinking feel like it\'s cheating in some way?Since the answers will be doing so, we should feel free to speak any of three languages. The argument is flawed because the author ...takes for granted that X (Assumption answers)fails to consider that Y (Objection answers)made this illegal move (Description answers)`\n  },\n  {\n    position: 85,\n    title: \'Most Supported (First Taste)\',\n    text: "Try these eight Level 1-3 Most Supported questions from tests 73 and 71. In general, Most Supported just gives us a paragraph of statements / information, and then the correct answer is the most derivable answer choice available.However, there are a few special variations of Most Supported:If it\'s Logical Completion (fill in the blank), think about a safely worded conclusion that would pull together the thoughts already mentioned. Look out for situations where they want us to Complete the Analogy. (Randomly, like 5 of the problems from these tests happen to be Logical Completion, but they aren\'t usually that common)If they\'re providing us with a Principle and asking us to Apply the Principle, pick an answer where the evidence matches the trigger of the principle, and the conclusion matches the outcome of the principle.If they\'re asking which Proposition / Generalization can be best supported, pick an answer that matches the situation described, but beware language that is Too Strong!\\n" +\n      "Be careful with overly strong/specific language in answer choices, because frequently we can\'t support that extremity or specificity. If there is a Comparison / Analogy, think about spelling out what similarity or difference would carryover from one situation to another."\n  },\n  {\n    position: 102,\n    title: \'Old / New + Implied + Undefined Target\',\n    text: `This set contains two Old / New passages from tests 66 and 70, as well as six questions testing What\'s Implied.Inference and Opinion are almost always phrased in a Most Supported degree. That "squishiness" tends to make the questions harder, as the correct answer either restates a single idea from the passage (but in really disguised linguistic fashion), or it synthesizes ideas into a gist-y but moderate sounding claim.These questions also vary in terms of whether there are Clue Words in the Question Stem that lead us to have a Defined or Semi-Defined target.The examples in this set almost all have an Undefined Target, i.e. they\'re totally open ended and don\'t warn us what parts of the passage might be tested. When we come up against an undefined target, we want to use "strength of language" as a valuable tool on our 1st pass. If an answer choice seems to have strong wording or a broad comparison then it has a pretty high burden of proof, so we consider that pretty "toxic" and try to bail from reading or thinking about such answers too much on a first pass. Try to find answers with more moderate language, more limited scope. If it sounds a little like cryptic / abstract / aloof legalese, then that\'s an inviting sign! Try to find supporting text for one of those answers, and then if you have to revisit one of the harsh ones \\n` +\n      "Attempt the passages and questions untimed. We\'ve already warned you that you can use an Old / New framework, so pay a lot of attention to where those Old / New foreshadowing clues are in the first paragraph. Once you know what the Old is, start making those mental containers for Old and New: the Old one is filled, you just need to reinforce it in your memory periodically. The New one is what you\'re reading with an appetite to fill. \ufeffPause as needed to cement your understanding of the Old and the New. This has to be in your words, not the passages, as much as possible (some science-y terms we might not have more casual, personal language for).When you\'re attempting questions, remember to be nervous about picking answers with strong wording or broad comparisons, unless you can find some text in the passage that justifies such a claim, or unless the other answer choices are also using that sort of strong language.\xa0\xa0"\n  },\n  {\n    position: 106,\n    title: \'Parallel Flaw\',\n    text: "In Logical Reasoning, we talk about there being 3 families:Assumption/Objection family, Inference family, and Match family, and then there are Paradox questions, which don\'t fit well into any of those.Within the Match family are these question types:Main Conclusion, Role, Method, and ParallelWithin the Assumption/Objection family are these question types:Necessary Assumption, Sufficient Assumption, Strengthen + Principle, Strengthen, Weaken, Evaluate, and FlawSo where do we put Parallel Flaw? It combines Parallel (from Match) and Flaw (from Assumption/Objection). Our task is to read an argument, evaluate its logic, and try to characterize the parts of the argument and their relationship to each other.Evaluating logic (figuring out what\'s wrong with an argument) is the province of Flaw questions. And taking an inventory of the number of premises, types of claims, strength of claims, and relationship between claims is the province of Parallel questions. \\n" +\n      \'Watch this video on Parallel Flaw Pay attention to high-level reasons we can eliminate answers, because fully engaging with all five answer choices on Parallel questions is tiring and time-consuming.\xa0\xa0\'\n  },\n  {\n    position: 113,\n    title: \'Comparative Passages + Relationship (set 2)\',\n    text: "This is a trio of comparative passages, from tests 67 - 69, as well as any Relationship questions that come with them (7 total).Relationship questions ask us to compare the passages to each other, so it\'s usually difficult to make much headway on them unless you\'ve already read both passages. Then, as you\'re starting to read Passage B (and throughout your reading of Passage B), pause to start trying to make connections about how the two passages related. They\'re at least partly analogous.Arguments by analogy tend to think, "Because X and Y are similar when it comes to Thing A, they\'re probably similar when it comes to Thing B". Necessary Assumption / Strengthen / Principle / Most Supported questions will want us to Complete the Analogy.Flaw and Weaken will want us to challenge this analogy by pointing to a potentially crucial difference (like maybe Thelma only likes east coast rap, Rodney\'s only likes west coast, and my playlist totally leaves out west coast rap like Dre, Snoop, Pac, NWA, etc.)\\n` +\n      `Try these 9 questions untimed, thinking through the analogies. We don\'t have to evaluate the argument in any way. No reason to think about what the author is assuming, or anything like that. Just find the conclusion. Cool, you found it? Are you sure? If we negated every answer choice and turned the question stem into "Which of the following, must be true", we\'d get the same correct answer.So if it fits your common sense better, you could think of a Must Be False question stem as saying, "For which answer, can I prove the opposite is true?" Usually these passages end with the author providing some recommendation or corrective, so just like Answer a Question and Present Debate and Old / New, we often don\'t hear the Author\'s voice or main point until the final paragraph.But in some cases, the author never provides a solution, and so our main point ends up sounding like a description of the Problem. Identifying FeaturesOne of the interesting parts of Problem / Solution passages is that we\'re very likely to get the Main Point in the final paragraph, because the author tends to spend two or three paragraphs acquainting us with a problematic situation.Some passages only describe a Problem. This is typical in Law passages, where an author might want to explore a thorny legal issue that doesn\'t have any clear answers right now.Some Humanities passages will feel like the author is simply complaining about something, without offering a better way. Similarly, we could think of these critique passages as Presenting a Problem, but never offering a solution.Sometimes, the author will present or evaluate other people\'s proposed Solutions. If the author implicitly agrees with someone else\'s solution, then she\'ll usually put it towards the end and offer no pushback. In other passages, though, the author will shoot down other people\'s potential solutions before proposing her own (or giving up that there is still no good solution).\\n" +\n      `Get 4 out of your last 5 correct, to pass this Level.If it doesn\'t happen within 30 mins, that\'s fine. (This will be heavily connected to picking a good Framework for the passage and thinking about what the big ideas are in that Framework)Better Question Stem Pre-Gaming -- are we able to locate the Support Window or even the specific answer to a question stem that either has keywords or asks a question we could answer in our own words, using our Big Picture understanding of the passage.Better Answer Choice Analysis -- can we seek out the vulnerabilities in each answer choice (usually wording that is overly Strong/Specific, wording that makes an Unknown Comparison, or unmentioned wording that is Out of Scope)? This drill is all about documenting our thought process at each stage so that if we get a question wrong or struggle to get it correct, we can be more precise with where we needed to improve our reading or thinking. \\n" +\n      "Pop open the Notepad panel and cover up the answer choices to the first question. Read the passageAs you\'re reading, or once you\'re done reading, highlight up to 3 sentences (and only those 3) as your understanding of where the most important Big Picture sentences are.For each question you then attempt,Start with the answer choices covered up by the NotepadAssuming that there\'s any way to anticipate an answer or to anticipate where in the passage the answer\'s supporting lines will come from, read what you need from the passage until you can make a prediction. Your prediction could be your own gist-y summary, it could be retrieving a specific fact from the passage, or it could be narrowing things down to a few lines or details within a certain paragraph.Once you\'ve recorded your prediction, minimize Notepad and select an answer (but don\'t hit confirm).Once you\'ve selected an answer, open Notepad again and type up your reason for getting rid of each wrong answer choice. If there\'s a dealbreaker word or phrase, just write that. Is there a more efficient or portable way to eliminate an answer than the one you wrote down?"\n  },\n  {\n    position: 191,\n    title: \'Humanities - Level 3\',\n    text: "Common FrameworksHumanities is most closely associated with the Highlight Noteworthy framework. A lot of these passages are just little biographies of an artist or art movement, with some emphasis placed on what makes them distinctive or noteworthy. The author almost always has a positive impression of any artist or movement she\'s profiling. If a common criticism of that artist is raised, a Humanities author will usually Challenge Position (clarifying a misconception, usually).\ufeffAnd then there are quite a few passages that critique something, either a specific point of view (Challenge Position) or some recent trend (which might work with Old / New or Problem w/o Solution).\\n" +\n      `Get 4 out of your last 5 correct, to pass this Level.If it doesn\'t happen within 30 mins, that\'s fine. Feel free to keep working at it if you\'re so inclined, or to just come back to it at another time.Big Picture Reading PracticeSee if there\'s any foreshadowing in that first paragraph, setting up an Old/New shift, or introducing some Position attributed to others that the author may Challenge, or a Question people are debating. If not -- if the author just starts talking about some artist or art movement, then it will probably just be a Highlight Noteworthy type passage.As you read, keep testing yourself on retention by looking away from the screen and seeing if you can comfortably say the Main Ideas in your own words.The author thinks this artist or trend is important because...The reason we care about this book / this study / this person / this movement / this situation is because...The problem or complication that the Author cares about is...The Old idea was... / The New idea is...The signature traits of this artist\'s style or how they differed themselves from their contemporaries/predecessors was ... (Optional) Deluxe Learning ModeThis takes longer, but makes a bigger difference on our brains. Use the NOTES panel (the page icon in the bottom left of the page pops open a NOTES panel you can move around) to record your thoughts. Big Picture RetentionWhen you\'re done reading the passage, cover up the passage and type in your memory of the big ideas. If you\'re finding that you thought you understood what you were reading, but it\'s very hard to remember what to write down once you\'re not looking at the passage anymore, that means that you\'re not doing enough self-summarizing yet. When we read big ideas, we pause on those sentences long enough to digest them and simplify them in our own personal wording. This process is what leads to strong retention. We have an easier time remembering our own words than remembering an LSAT author\'s.Pre-phrasingWhen you\'re ready to start working through actual questions, use the NOTES panel to cover up the answer choices. If the question stem has no keywords, feel free to write nothing, or "no pre-phrase", or "beware strong language on first pass".Answer Evaluation Resize the NOTES panel so that you can see answers again, and when you pick your answer, type into the NOTES panel where your supporting text was found (you might need more than one sentence to support your answer, but usually it\'s just one sentence). (maybe once in a blue moon, you\'d have two "true" answers, where you\'d have to ask which one\'s better.)The most common correct answer is Premise or some other way of describing Supporting Idea.Easier Role questions will stick to classic language like Premise and Conclusion, whereas harder Role questions will often switch to less familiar abstract language or synonyms.Main Conclusion - the claim the author seeks to establish, a generalization supported by evidence, the only conclusionPremise - support, partial support (just means there\'s more than one premise), evidence, illustration of, example of, unsupported premiseIntermediate Conclusion - subsidiary conclusion, supported premise, a conclusion but not the main conclusion, a statement for which some support is provided but is used to support the main conclusion\ufeffOpposing Position - the view the argument is designed to discredit, the claim the author attempts to show is false\\n` +\n      "Get 4 out of your last 5 correct,to pass this level.incorrect answers on RoleWrong Ingredient - these describe something in the paragraph, but not the claim we were asked aboutToo Strong - some answers that about an idea being required or sufficient for the conclusionDidn\'t Happen - these reference something that never happened in the paragraphWrong Conclusion - lots of wrong answers correctly call the claim a Premise but then say it\'s supporting some idea that doesn\'t match the argument\'s Conclusion"\n  },\n  {\n    position: 198,\n    title: \'Explain Curious Fact (Medium) Set 1\',\n    text: "This set has four Weaken, a Necessary Assumption, and a Strengthen question.The evidence presents some Curious Fact (an asymmetric comparison like a correlation, a statistical change, or a difference between two groups or situations)The author\'s conclusion will state or assume one possible Causal Explanation for this curious fact. The correct answer (on any Assumption / Objection Family question type) will deal either with an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact or with the plausibility of the Author\'s Explanation.\\n" +\n      `Try these 6 questions in 9 minutes(1.5x = 14 mins, 2x = 18 mins)What is the Curious Fact? (ask it as a question)what language tips us off?What is the Author\'s Explanation / Hypothesis?Is there a causal verb in the conclusion? Remember to spell out every link in the causal chain that author is envisioning, from initial Cause to ultimate Effect. Does the correct answer deal with an Alternate Explanation?If so, Reverse Causality or Third Factor?Or does it address the plausibility of the Author\'s Explanation?If no, does it use "covariation" data points, or some other means? (covariation means stuff like No Cause, No Effect as a strengthener, or stuff like Cause w/o Effect / Effect w/o Cause as a weakener)`\n  },\n  {\n    position: 199,\n    title: \'Law - Level 3\',\n    text: "Common FrameworksThe most common frameworks in Law passages are Problem / Solution and Present Debate. Law passages are often about thorny legal issues with no clear solution. They\'ll come in a few forms:Describe Problem (no solutions presented)Problem, someone else\'s Solution, author unsatisfiedProblem, someone else\'s Solution, author on boardProblem, author\'s SolutionWithin Debate passages, there are also a few variations. When an author brings up two or more points of view (besides her own) on a subject, she might:Stay neutralAgree with one side over the otherIntroduce a third position that isn\'t quite either side of the debateBoth of these frameworks can overlap with an Old / New framework, since much of the time the OLD will feel like the Problem and the NEW will be the Solution (some steps the legal community is taking to address an emerging issue). Use the NOTES panel (the page icon in the bottom left of …905 tokens truncated…3\',\n    text: `Main Conclusion stimulus tendenciesLSAC is seeking to make it harder than usual to find the Conclusion. So it\'s very rare to see the Conclusion be the final claim, prefaced by anything obvious like Therefore / Thus / So.Instead, in more than 90% of Main Conclusion questions, the conclusion appears earlier than the Supporting Idea(s). Because of this, we prime our brain to listen for a potential First Sentence or Rebuttal style conclusion.Other times, the Conclusion will be indirectly revealed by Support Indicator like "for, after all, to see this". On easier questions, they might use an obvious Support indicator like "since" or "because".Sometimes, our only clue about where the conclusion is will be an Opinion Indicator like "probably, apparently, evidently". Beware that there may be Intermediate Conclusions. They will pass the Support test, because they will have their own premise. But they are there to support the Main Conclusion.Beware that there may be Causal-Indicator words that look like Conclusion-Indicator words. Usually when we see "thus, therefore, hence, so" that word indicates a Premise → Conclusion relationship, but we will sometimes see them used to indicate a Cause ⇢ Effect relationship.REASONINGSharon is a very graceful dancer. Thus, she probably studied ballet growing up.CAUSALITYSharon fell off her roof and thus broke her leg.\\n` +\n      `Get 4 out of your last 5 correct,to pass this Level for Main Conclusioncorrect answerThe correct answer just reproduces the meaning of the Conclusion. Sometimes it\'s a verbatim regurgitation. More commonly, they use synonyms or inverted syntax to present an equivalent meaning that still looks a little different.f.e. if the conclusion appeared in the argument as "not all tornadoes should be avoided", then an equivalent claim would be "some tornadoes should not be avoided".If you didn\'t already do the 2-part Conclusion Check when you were first reading the argument and determining which claim is the conclusion, you can do it now (or again) --is this answer expressing an Opinion from our Author? \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0(facts ≠ conclusions)was this answer Supported by at least one explicit claim?incorrect answersPremiseLast Claim Trap (they know that we wish for the last claim to be the Conclusion)Intermediate ConclusionWhat Next (these present a claim that was never said, but they don\'t like the next thing the author would probably say)Necessary Assumption (these feel tempting because we can tell that they are a correct inference about the author\'s thinking, but the Conclusion is an explicit claim, whereas these assumptions are implicit; they were never said)`\n  },\n  {\n    position: 236,\n    title: \'Principle-Strengthen - Level 3\',\n    text: \'Get 4 out of your last 5 correct,to pass this Level.question stem keywordsprinciple, if valid / if assumed / if established, most justifies, most supportsexamplesWhich principle, if valid, most justifies the reasoning in the argument?Which principle, if established, most helps to justify the decision?\\n\' +\n      `Principle-Strengthen + Principles in AnswersFind the CONCLUSION and the EVIDENCE.Pre-phrase "IF premise, THEN conclusion".The correct answer should sound like 1/2 Premise language, 1/2 Conclusion language.Try to get rid of answer choices quickly if they don\'t have Conclusion languageAlso be wary of answers that put the Conclusion on the left side of arrow, or that say "not the Conclusion" on the right of the arrow.If there are competing interests being weighted against each other, the correct answer may rank one thing as more important than another.`\n  },\n  {\n    position: 239,\n    title: \'Sufficient Assumption - Level 3\',\n    text: \'Get 4 out of your last 5 correctto pass Level 3 for Sufficient Assumption. \\n\' +\n      "Remember, if there\'s a New Term that only appears in the Conclusion, that idea must be in the correct answer. Sufficient Assumption is unlike other question types in that you spend more time upfront dissecting the argument and figuring out what you want. By the time you get to answers, you shouldn\'t be weighing which one you like more or less. We\'re less likely to think we\'re supposed to be looking at the internal logic of the argument and more likely to think that we\'re going to be weighing the impact of brand new considerations in the answers.However, Sufficient Assumption is only about the internal logic. So when you combine Sufficient Assumption with Science, you might feel your brain engaging with the story, when our attention needs to stay with the logical features.If there is a New Concept in the Conclusion, we know that idea has to be in the correct answer (and usually will be referred to in verbatim language). If the argument seems pretty internally solid, try to think of a possible objection:\xa0\xa0"given [this evidence], how could it still be possible that [conclusion is false]?"If we can think of a possible objection, then we know the correct answer will have to rule out that objection. \\n` +\n      `Try all 6 problems untimed.Make use of the Notepad popup. Click on the icon in the lower left and move / resize the Notes window so that it covers up your answer choices.Try to make a specific prediction about what the answer should say / do. Sometimes you might predict an "If Premise, Then Conclusion" link. Sometimes you might think, "it has to rule out this Objection". If you can\'t figure out the whole missing link, at least focus on the wording from the Conclusion that you need to prove.Once you see the correct answer, revisit your prediction. Do you think you could have anticipated the correct answer if you had read the paragraph differently? Or is this correct answer more one you just have to read and interpret on the fly?Remember that on Sufficient Assumption, the correct answer, when added to our evidence, allows us to mathematically derive the conclusion.`\n  },\n  {\n    position: 254,\n    title: \'Sufficient Assumption - Level 4\',\n    text: \'Get 4 out of your last 5 correctto pass Level 4 for Sufficient Assumption. \\n\' +\n      "Remember, if there\'s a New Term that only appears in the Conclusion, that idea must be in the correct answer. Try to solve for the Missing Link or Missing Idea before you get to the answer choices. \ufeffIf you don\'t see what idea would be missing, go into Objection mode -- how could we possibly argue that the conclusion is wrong? If we can think of an objection, then the correct answer needs to rule out our Objection (and all other objections like it)."\n  },\n  {\n    position: 256,\n    title: \'Theme / Example + Five Questions\',\n    text: "This set contains two Theme / Example passages from tests 128 and 145, as well as their accompanying Five Questions questions (2 total). The framework doesn\'t actually matter to you for this activity, though, because this is not a big picture question type. It\'s a super narrow detail hunt.Five Questions questions are stupidly named by us, because you have to say the word questions twice. They sound like this:The passage provides information sufficient to answer which of the following questions?Each answer choice poses a question. If we can find the answer to that question in the passage, then we pick that answer!These are total scavenger hunts. The correct answer usually is not addressing any important part of the passage or meaningful detail. The five answers will use keywords from the passage to make them sound plausible.If we want to re-read the sentences where these keywords were used, we have to go hunting through potentially five different areas of the passage. \\n" +\n      "Attempt the two questions, untimed. Five Questions involves reverse engineering, from each answer choice, what part of the passage they\'re even talking about. Try to play around with using the search bar to assist you with searching. Look for some searchable keyword within each answer choice that could bring you to the relevant sentence of the passage. There, you can assess whether or not you really have the means to answer the question posed in that answer choice.If you\'d rather practice your big picture reading on Theme / Example, then read the whole passage. But otherwise, practice your scan/search skills by diving immediately into researching each answer choice, without reading the passage first."\n  },\n  {\n    position: 259,\n    title: \'Science + Strengthen / Weaken\',\n    text: " # of questions:\xa0\xa08 Question Type: Strengthen / Weaken\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Difficulty Level: 4 and 5\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Tests: pt 23 - 44\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Theme:\xa0\xa0science-heavy stimulusThis question set contains 8 tough questions, all level 4-5, Strengthen / Weaken, with Science-heavy paragraphs. These are the questions that can become quicksand time-suckers. We try to buy time on easier questions so that we have adequate time to think about these.Ultimately, the gross vernacular of science questions is just a distraction. We\'re still playing the same old reasoning games, so pay more attention to reasoning patterns and right/wrong answer tendencies for that question type, and pay less attention to getting a thorough understanding of whatever scientific concept is being discussed.\\n" +\n      `Choose a study goal\xa0\xa0Untimed:\xa0\xa0Focus on perfect accuracyTimed:\xa0\xa012 mins keep-it-movingFor Weaken questions, focus on the Anti-Conclusion. After you read the argument, frame your goal by saying:\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Given\xa0\xa0this evidenceHow can I still argue \xa0\xa0the anti-conclusion?For Strengthen questions, remember that when you\'re dealing with scientific hypotheses, you can strengthen by either Ruling Out an Alternate Hypothesis, or you can Boost the Plausibility of the Author\'s Hypothesis.For Strengthen + Principle, focus on finding an answer that works like "If evidence, then conclusion". The goal is to think about how Keywords in the Question Stem (or the absence thereof) help to determine where we look in the passage for potential supporting text.We often nickname the available supporting text the "Support Window". Some questions have a very narrow support window (defined target), some have more of a regional one (semi-defined target), and some seem to apply to the whole passage (undefined target).\\n\' +\n      "Try these four questions, untimedPay attention to the question stems to see whether we\'re being tested on what\'s stated or what\'s implied:Stated (according to the passage, information sufficient to answer which question, indicates, says, mentions)Implied (most supported, suggests, most likely to agree, most reasonably inferred)And pay attention to the difference in Support Windowthe whole passage is up for grabs (undefined target)a certain paragraph is being tested (semi-defined target)the keywords send us to 1 or 2 specific lines (defined target)"\n  },\n  {\n    position: 263,\n    title: \'Principle-Strengthen + Application (mini-set)\',\n    text: `Find the gap between a Rule and its Applicationon these 2 Principle-Strengthen questions(example)PRINCIPLE  Lies are justified if they do more good than harm.APPLICATION  Jason falsely claimed that Sharon has a driver\'s license to spare her getting mocked by her friends. Since he did manage to spare her the mockery, he was justified in lying.In order to use this Rule to prove that a lie was justified, we have to establish the trigger:\xa0\xa0the lie did more good than harmSo the correct answer would need to convince us that "keeping Sharon from getting mocked = did more good than harm".\\n` +\n      "Try these two questions, untimed,Focus on predicting what you want before you look at answers.Think about each Principle as having some criteria that must be met to trigger the rule, and having an outcome that matches up with the Application\'s conclusion. The Application will conclude the right side of the Principle. We\'re just being tested on how the Evidence in the Application paragraph failed to clearly establish the trigger (left side) of the Principle. Think about which part(s) of the Principle\'s trigger wasn\'t clearly established, and keep that mantra in your head as you consider answer choices."\n  },\n  {\n    position: 265,\n    title: \'Principle-Strengthen - Level 4\',\n    text: \'Get 4 out of your last 5 correct,to pass this Level.question stem keywordsprinciple, if valid / if assumed / if established, most justifies, most supportsexamplesWhich principle, if valid, most justifies the reasoning in the argument?Which principle, if established, most helps to justify the decision?\\n\' +\n      `Principle-Strengthen Find the CONCLUSION and the EVIDENCE.Pre-phrase "IF premise, THEN conclusion".The correct answer should sound like 1/2 Premise language, 1/2 Conclusion language.Try to get rid of answer choices quickly on the first pass, if they don\'t have Conclusion languageAlso be wary of answers that put the Conclusion on the left side of arrow, or that say "not the Conclusion" on the right of the arrow.If there are competing interests being weighted against each other, the correct answer may rank one thing as more important than another.`\n  },\n  {\n    position: 266,\n    title: \'Humanities - Level 4\',\n    text: "Common FrameworksHumanities is most closely associated with the Highlight Noteworthy framework. A lot of these passages are just little biographies of an artist or art movement, with some emphasis placed on what makes them distinctive or noteworthy. Feel free to keep working at it if you\'re so inclined, or to just come back to it at another time.Big Picture Reading PracticeSee if there\'s any foreshadowing in that first paragraph, setting up an Old/New shift, or introducing some Position attributed to others that the author may Challenge, or a Question people are debating. When we read big ideas, we pause on those sentences long enough to digest them and simplify them in our own personal wording. This process is what leads to strong retention. We have an easier time remembering our own words than remembering an LSAT author\'s.Pre-phrasingWhen you\'re ready to start working through actual questions, use the NOTES panel to cover up the answer choices. These two separate cases share some relationship, so they are analogous in at least one respect. Analogies show up a lot on Method of reasoning questions, which ask us to characterize the type of evidence or type of move the author used. When we see a fill-in-the-blank question (aka Logical Completion), the paragraph is leading us to some final idea, and they frequently use a Complete the Analogy type structure, as I did at the top of this page. When we see analogies show up in the Assumption Family, they tend to go like this: "Because X and Y are similar when it comes to Thing A, they\'re probably also similar when it comes to Thing B". Five years ago, my family went to Lake Crocus and I didn\'t have any fun. Thus, I will not have any fun when my family goes to visit Lake Crocus this summer. The author has established one similarity "both vacations are at the same location" and is assuming a second similarity, "both vacations will be not-fun". Flaw and Weaken will want us to challenge this analogy by pointing to a potentially meaningful difference. Necessary Assumption will rule out salient differences, and Strengthen will add more similarity, make them seem more Fair to Compare. \\n` +\n      \'Try these 8 questions untimed, thinking through the analogies. What are the two separate cases? What is the common principle? What language cues exist to telegraph that the author is making a Comparison / Analogy?Do the two cases seem "fair to compare" or do you think there could be an important difference between the two cases that calls into question the implied similarity. EXAMPLEWhen people go to casinos, they gamble with their money, spending as much as they can stand to lose, hoping for the excitement of a jackpot. Similarly, when a fisherman goes out on Lake Crocus for the better part of the day, hoping for the excitement of a big catch, ________ .How would we carry through a trait or relationship from the dating situation to the LSAT tutor situation? Something like,these fisherman are gambling with their time, spending as much of it as they can stand to lose\'\n  },\n  {\n    position: 276,\n    title: \'Law + Comparative Passages\',\n    text: "Try this pair of Law passages.They also happen to both be in Comparative Passage format. On Comparative Passage sets, as we read our 2nd passage, we want to be relating it back to the 1st passage, finding ways in which they\'re similar or different:TopicTone / AttitudeWide vs. Narrow ScopePurpose / MethodConclusions / EvidenceComplementary / AdversarialLaw passages, in general, highlight problems or ambiguities in the law, frequently presenting a debate or a problem without offering a clear remedy.\\n" +\n      `GoalsBecause we care most about the relationship between passages, we can potentially care less about thinking of frameworks for each individual passage.After we\'ve read one of the two passages, if we want, we can flip through the question and see what selections or eliminations are possible (before being "tainted"" by the second one). If we\'ve read passage A and a question is only asking about Passage A, we can answer it. And if a question is asking something like, "Which of the following is a central purpose of each passage?", then we can eliminate all the answers that don\'t apply to the passage we\'ve read. `\n  },\n  {\n    position: 277,\n    title: \'Law - Level 4\',\n    text: "Common FrameworksThe most common frameworks in Law passages are Problem / Solution and Present Debate. Law passages are often about thorny legal issues with no clear solution.
