5\n\t\t\t\t18572 heading Principle-Conform: Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t18573 text Principle-Conform: Level 5\n\t\t\t\t18574 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t18575 text 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t18576 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t18577 text Info\n\t\t\t\t18578 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t18579 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t18580 container\n\t\t\t\t\t18581 text There are three varieties of \n\t\t\t\t\t18582 text Principle-Conform\n\t\t\t\t\t18583 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t18584 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t18585 text • The stimulus is a principle (or pair of principles)\n\t\t\t\t\t\t18586 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t18587 text • The answers are principles\n\t\t\t\t\t\t18588 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t18589 text • There are no explicit principles, just implied/illustrated ones\n\t\t\t\t\t18590 text Principles in Stimulus\n\t\t\t\t\t18591 text When the stimulus is providing an explicit principle (or two), we\'re usually being tested on our ability to apply a conditional rule. \n\t\t\t\t\t18592 text To find an answer that Conforms to this principle, we want an answer where the situation described matches the Trigger of the principle, and the judgment concluded matches the Outcome of the principle. (Even when the principles aren\'t expressed as conditionals, there will still usually be two things we need to make sure match up).\n\t\t\t\t\t18593 text Principles in Answers\n\t\t\t\t\t18594 text It\'s essentially the same mindset as a Principle-Strengthen question. We read the argument and then anticipate the principle underlying the argument by pre-phrasing "IF evidence, THEN conclusion". We expect the correct answer to \n\t\t\t\t\t18595 text Link \n\t\t\t\t\t18596 text language from the Evidence to the Conclusion\'s language.\xa0All that\'s different is that because the question stem says \n\t\t\t\t\t18597 text conform \n\t\t\t\t\t18598 text to the author\'s reasoning, we can\'t pick an answer that\'s overly strong. (That usually doesn\'t matter, but occasionally it does)\n\t\t\t\t\t18599 text Implicit Principles\n\t\t\t\t\t18600 text These feel similar to Parallel reasoning questions, because we\'re given an argument in the stimulus, and then each answer choice is its own argument on its own unique topic. We\'re looking for an underlying similarity to connect the correct answer to the original argument.\n\t\t\t\t\t18601 text On Parallel questions, those similarities come more in the form of technical / structural similarities (i.e. "Since the original argument had a \n\t\t\t\t\t18602 text Most \n\t\t\t\t\t18603 text premise and a \n\t\t\t\t\t18604 text Some \n\t\t\t\t\t18605 text premise, the correct answer\'s argument will also have those features").\n\t\t\t\t\t18606 text But with Principle-Conform it\'s more about the underlying gist or rule-of-thumb. We don\'t try to diagram the arguments. We just want to articulate a general moral to the story or operating principle that\'s guiding the author\'s thinking, and then we try to find an answer that matches that.\n\t\t\t\t18607 container\n\t\t\t\t\t18608 text Get 4 of your last 5 correct, \n\t\t\t\t\t18609 text untimed\n\t\t\t\t\t18610 text , to pass this \n\t\t\t\t\t18611 text level\n\t\t\t\t\t18612 text .\n\t\t\t\t18613 image Speed Drill - Level 2\n\t\t\t\t18614 heading Speed Drill - Level 2, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t18615 text Speed Drill - Level 2\n\t\t\t\t18616 text Pacing\n\t\t\t\t18617 text 45 mins\n\t\t\t\t18618 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t18619 text Info\n\t\t\t\t18620 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t18621 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t18622 container\n\t\t\t\t\t18623 text This is a trio of \n\t\t\t\t\t18624 text level 2\n\t\t\t\t\t18625 text  passages from tests 62, 64, 69. There\'s a \n\t\t\t\t\t18626 text Present Debate\n\t\t\t\t\t18627 text , an \n\t\t\t\t\t18628 text Old / New\n\t\t\t\t\t18629 text , and a \n\t\t\t\t\t18630 text Problem / Solution\n\t\t\t\t\t18631 text  passage, although you could probably see all three as Problem / Solution, if you prefer.\n\t\t\t\t\t18632 text The goal of this exercise is to practice a sustained, brisk "speedwalking" pace. When the test is offering us its easier items, we need to act like it.\n\t\t\t\t\t18633 text We need to try pushing our pace so that we can bank some extra time to spend on the hardest parts of a section.\n\t\t\t\t18634 container\n\t\t\t\t\t18635 text Set yourself an appropriate time limit.\n\t\t\t\t\t18636 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t18637 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t18638 text • If you aren\'t yet used to finishing all four passages with enough time, give yourself  27  mins for this threesome. \n\t\t\t\t\t18639 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t18640 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t18641 text • If you tend to get through all four, then try doing them in  22  mins. \n\t\t\t\t\t18642 text Either way, keep your eye on the clock and have a guess for all 21 Q\'s (even if it\'s a blind guess). \n\t\t\t\t\t18643 text The time limit is supposed to force us into experimenting with new behaviors:\n\t\t\t\t\t18644 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t18645 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t18646 text • when you have high confidence about an answer choice, pick it and move on without worrying about reading all the other answers you haven\'t seen yet. (high confidence comes when we find an answer choice that matches the  meaning  of a line in the passage, but an exact  language  match usually means a trap answer. but  doesn\'t  match up with language in the passage, but we can tell LSAT has put some work into disguising it with synonyms or different syntax. \n\t\t\t\t\t18647 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t18648 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t18649 text • if you get four or five words into an answer choice and already see something you don\'t like, get out of there. we need to conserve time and mental energy by not processing the full sentence of every answer choice. find  earlier  reasons to disqualify an answer.\n\t\t\t\t\t18650 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t18651 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t18652 text • get the passage read in 2.5 minutes or less. be content to simply determine the topic and framework, find the ideas that fill your framework boxes, and don\'t worry about grabbing too much else. Read the first paragraph carefully, and read the 1st sentence of other paragraphs carefully, and read any  pivot  sentences ( but, yet, however ) carefully. Let the rest of it breeze by.\n\t\t\t\t\t18653 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t18654 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t18655 text • skip the worst problem in each passage set. we will tend to overspend time on that even though we have a lower average accuracy on that problem, so it\'s a bad value.\n\t\t\t\t\t18656 text Hit SUBMIT SET when the timer runs out. Then take a 2nd untimed look at the questions and explanations.\n\t\t\t\t18657 image Role - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t18658 heading Role - Level 5, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t18659 text Role - Level 5\n\t\t\t\t18660 text Level Drill\n\t\t\t\t18661 text 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t18662 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t18663 text Info\n\t\t\t\t18664 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t18665 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t18666 container\n\t\t\t\t\t18667 text On harder \n\t\t\t\t\t18668 text Role \n\t\t\t\t\t18669 text questions, we\'re likely to see a couple patterns emerge:\n\t\t\t\t\t18670 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t18671 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t18672 text • Intermediate Conclusion?  Many of the harder problems test the existence of an Intermediate Conclusion, even if the claim we\'re being asked about isn\'t itself that. Answer choices describing a Premise might differ by saying, "It\'s provides direct support for the Conclusion" vs. "It provide support for a claim that then provides direct support for the Conclusion".\n\t\t\t\t\t18673 text To assess whether a claim is or isn\'t an Intermediate Conclusion, we want to ask ourselves, "\n\t\t\t\t\t18674 text Is there\n\t\t\t\t\t18675 text Support\n\t\t\t\t\t18676 text  for this claim? Why should we believe this claim? Does anything else in the paragraph sound like it\'s answering that question?"\n\t\t\t\t\t18677 text Often, when there \n\t\t\t\t\t18678 text isn\'t \n\t\t\t\t\t18679 text a supporting idea present and thus the claim you\'re examining is really just a Premise, it\'s useful to think about how \n\t\t\t\t\t18680 text you\n\t\t\t\t\t18681 text would support that claim.\n\t\t\t\t\t18682 text If you\'re asking yourself, "Was the claim \n\t\t\t\t\t18683 text You shouldn\'t tell jokes at a funeral \n\t\t\t\t\t18684 text supported?" Supply your own answer, just get your brain hearing what actual support would sound like:\xa0\xa0"you shouldn\'t tell jokes at a funeral \n\t\t\t\t\t18685 text because\n\t\t\t\t\t18686 text ... funerals are a somber occasion and telling jokes makes it seem like you\'re not respecting the gravity of the situation". By articulating what support would sound like, you can sometimes help strengthen your conviction that no support was provided, if you\'re not seeing any claims like that.\n\t\t\t\t\t18687 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t18688 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t18689 text • Relational language, rather than classic Argument Role language.  Harder problems tend to supply fewer answers with recognizable terms like "Premise, Conclusion, Intermediate Conclusion" and either use more complicated abstract phrases to signify the same idea, or they don\'t really concern themselves with those labels at all. Instead, they just conversationally describe how the claims relate to each other, almost more like a  Method  of reasoning question. \n\t\t\t\t18690 container\n\t\t\t\t\t18691 text Get 4 out of your last 5 correct,\n\t\t\t\t\t18692 text to pass this level.\n\t\t\t\t18693 image Speedwalking LR (set 2)\n\t\t\t\t18694 heading Speedwalking LR (set 2), Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t18695 text Speedwalking LR (set 2)\n\t\t\t\t18696 text Pacing\n\t\t\t\t18697 text 45 mins\n\t\t\t\t18698 button Info\n\t\t\t\t\t18699 text Info\n\t\t\t\t18700 link Description: Start, Value: …\n\t\t\t\t18701 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t18702 container\n\t\t\t\t\t18703 text LENGTH\n\t\t\t\t\t18704 text  -- 15 Q\'s, 15 minutes (1.5x = 22, 2x = 30)\n\t\t\t\t\t18705 text TYPES\n\t\t\t\t\t18706 text  -- Paradox, Flaw, Role, Main Conclusion, Necessary Assumption, Sufficient Assumption, Strengthen, Weaken, Method, and Must Be True.\n\t\t\t\t\t18707 text LEVEL\n\t\t\t\t\t18708 text  -- 1\n\t\t\t\t\t18709 text Wait a sec -- these are all level 1? I thought this activity was listed as level 5?\n\t\t\t\t\t18710 text Yes, because the goal is something a level 5 student needs to work on:\xa0\xa0be able to quickly take care of easier questions, so that you\'ll have more time and brainpower in reserves for the harder, more flexible thinking questions in the section.\n\t\t\t\t\t18711 text Given how many subtle reading traps there are on LSAT, it\'s sometimes difficult to ever let yourself believe that an answer you find appealing is correct. "It\'s never this easy", we might think. But, sure it is! Sometimes it really is that easy. We need to improve our ability to \n\t\t\t\t\t18712 text let the easy be easy\n\t\t\t\t\t18713 text .\n\t\t\t\t\t18714 text And we need to develop enough self-trust while we\'re doing easier problems that we can pick up our pace when possible.\n\t\t\t\t18715 container\n\t\t\t\t\t18716 text Try to get through these 15 questions in 15 mins. Keep yourself going at a brisk pace. When you have a strong idea of what you\'re looking for (like on Main Conclusion, Role, Sufficient Assumption, Flaw), try to be proactive about scanning for and finding your answer, rather than reading all five choices start to finish.\n\t\t\t\t\t18717 text However, on tasks where we compare the impact of new information (like Paradox, Strengthen, Weaken), we may still need to use more time to consider all five answers.\n\t\t\t\t\t18718 text If your thinking feels unfinished on any of them, flag them as you go (so that you can maintain your brisk pace), and then take a second look at them after the timer goes off before you check your answer / the explanation.\n\t\t\t\t18719 image PrepTest 141 - Section 3\n\t\t\t\t18720 heading PrepTest 141 - Section 3, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t18721 text PrepTest 141 - Section 3\n\t\t\t\t18722 text Timed Section 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t18723 button Take Section\n\t\t\t\t\t18724 text Take Section\n\t\t\t\t18725 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t18726 image PrepTest 143 - Section 1\n\t\t\t\t18727 heading PrepTest 143 - Section 1, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t18728 text PrepTest 143 - Section 1\n\t\t\t\t18729 text Timed Section 1 hr, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t18730 button Take Section\n\t\t\t\t\t18731 text Take Section\n\t\t\t\t18732 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t18733 image PrepTest 156\n\t\t\t\t18734 heading PrepTest 156, Value: 6\n\t\t\t\t\t18735 text PrepTest 156\n\t\t\t\t18736 text Practice Test 4 hrs, 30 mins\n\t\t\t\t18737 button Take Test\n\t\t\t\t\t18738 text Take Test\n\t\t\t\t18739 text \uf34c\n\t\t\t\t18740 button \uf2c2\n\t\t\t\t\t18741 text \uf2c2\n\t\t\t18742 container\n\t\t\t\t18743 heading Week 15, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t18744 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t18745 text Week  15\n\t\t\t\t18746 text January 3rd - 9th, 2027\n\t\t\t\t18747 text Est. class="d-inline-flex flex-column ml-3"><h6 class="item_sub-text_dark mb-1">Find the Conclusion</h6><p class="text-muted d-block mb-0">Flashcards</p></div></div><div class="item_sub item_time">10 la-trash"></i></div></div><div class="schedule_item-expand "><div class="row pb-4"><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pr-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">~70% of the paragraphs we read in LR are labeled </span><strong class="ql-size-large">arguments</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> or </span><strong class="ql-size-large">reasoning. </strong></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">What do those words mean? </span></p><p><br></p><p class="ql-indent-2"><span class="ql-size-large">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</span><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);">A</span><span class="ql-size-large"> </span><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);">claim </span><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">that is</span><span class="ql-size-large">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;supported by some </span><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(193, 53, 53);">other claim</span><span class="ql-size-large">(s)</span></p><p class="ql-indent-2"><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(21, 134, 202);"><em>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Conclusion</em></strong><strong class="ql-size-large"><em>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</em></strong><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(193, 53, 53);"><em>Evidence, Premise, Support</em></strong><strong class="ql-size-large"><em> </em></strong></p><p class="ql-align-center"><span style="color: rgb(183, 186, 189);">____________________________________________________________________</span></p><p><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">To analyze an argument (which we do on 70% of LR questions), our first step is to find the Conclusion and its Supporting Idea(s). In most cases there is more than one Supporting Idea, but often there is only one premise. In a small percent of cases, there is more than one Conclusion. In those cases, there is a Main Conclusion that is supported by an Intermediate Conclusion, which is supported by its own premise. </span></p><p class="ql-align-center"><span style="color: rgb(183, 186, 189);">____________________________________________________________________</span></p><p><br></p><p class="ql-align-center"><span class="ql-size-large">THE CONCLUSION TESTS</span></p><p><br></p><ul><li class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">Is it</span><em class="ql-size-large"> </em><strong class="ql-size-large"><em>supported</em></strong><em class="ql-size-large"> </em><span class="ql-size-large">by some other claim?</span></li></ul><p class="ql-indent-2"><span class="ql-size-large">(If we\'re looking at a Conclusion and we ask, "</span><em class="ql-size-large">Why should I believe that?</em><span class="ql-size-large">", we will be able to point to at least one explicit supporting idea in the stimulus.)</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><ul><li class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">Is it the </span><strong class="ql-size-large">author\'s</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> </span><strong class="ql-size-large">opinion</strong><span class="ql-size-large">?</span></li></ul><p class="ql-indent-2"><span class="ql-size-large">(Factual claims and other people\'s opinions are almost never conclusions)</span></p><p><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">Note: to say that a claim is supported doesn\'t mean the argument </span><em class="ql-size-large">proved </em><span class="ql-size-large">the claim. The support doesn\'t have to be compelling or dispositive (fancy legal word meaning </span><em class="ql-size-large">it definitively settles the matter</em><span class="ql-size-large">). It just has to feel like an idea the author thinks will help persuade us of her conclusion. </span></p><p class="ql-indent-1 ql-align-center"><span style="color: rgb(183, 186, 189);">____________________________________________________________________</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1 ql-align-center"><br></p><h4 class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">Use </span><strong class="ql-size-large">keywords</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> whenever possible. </span></h4><h6 class="ql-indent-1"><br></h6><p class="ql-indent-2"><strong style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);" class="ql-size-large">CONCLUSION: </strong><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">so, thus, therefore, hence, it follows</span></p><p class="ql-indent-2"><strong style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);" class="ql-size-large">PIVOT: </strong><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">but, yet, however</span></p><p class="ql-indent-2"><strong style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);" class="ql-size-large">OPINION: </strong><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">clearly, obviously, should, probably, evidently</span></p><p class="ql-indent-2"><strong style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);" class="ql-size-large">SUPPORT: </strong><span style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);" class="ql-size-large"> (F.A.B.S.) for, after all, because, since</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span style="color: rgb(87, 89, 98);" class="ql-size-large">Support words </span><em style="color: rgb(87, 89, 98);" class="ql-size-large">indirectly</em><span style="color: rgb(87, 89, 98);" class="ql-size-large"> show us the Conclusion. The Conclusion is next door to them. If a claim is prefaced by FABS (for, after all, because, since), then it is </span><span style="color: rgb(193, 53, 53);" class="ql-size-large">Support</span><span style="color: rgb(87, 89, 98);" class="ql-size-large"> for a </span><span style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);" class="ql-size-large">Conclusion</span><span style="color: rgb(87, 89, 98);" class="ql-size-large"> that came right before or right after.</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><ul><li class="ql-indent-1"><strong style="color: rgb(193, 53, 53);" class="ql-size-large">Since</strong><span style="color: rgb(193, 53, 53);" class="ql-size-large"> </span><span class="ql-size-large">you like tea, </span><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);">you should try boba.</span></li><li class="ql-indent-1"><span style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);" class="ql-size-large">You should try boba. </span><strong style="color: rgb(193, 53, 53);" class="ql-size-large">because</strong><span style="color: rgb(193, 53, 53);" class="ql-size-large"> </span><span class="ql-size-large">you like tea. </span></li><li class="ql-indent-1"><span style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);" class="ql-size-large">You should try boba. </span><strong style="color: rgb(193, 53, 53);" class="ql-size-large">After all, </strong><span class="ql-size-large">you like tea. </span></li><li class="ql-indent-1"><span style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);" class="ql-size-large">You should try boba, </span><strong style="color: rgb(193, 53, 53);" class="ql-size-large">for </strong><span class="ql-size-large">you like tea. </span></li></ul></div></div></div></div><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pl-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><p class="ql-align-center"><span class="ql-size-huge">Take </span><strong class="ql-size-huge">7 minutes</strong><span class="ql-size-huge"> to try these flashcards.</span></p><p><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">Read each argument and </span><strong class="ql-size-large">identify</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> which of its explicit claims would be the </span><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);">Main Conclusion</strong><span class="ql-size-large">.</span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div><div src="https://assets.lsatlab.com/uploads/2021/08/Learn-A-Pattern_LR.png" alt="First Sentence Conclusions"></div><div class="d-inline-flex flex-column ml-3"><h6 class="item_sub-text_dark mb-1">First item_type">Patterns</div><div class="item_sub item_arrow"><i class="la la-angle-down"></i></div><div class="item_sub item_delete"><i class="la la-trash"></i></div></div><div class="schedule_item-expand "><div class="row pb-4"><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pr-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">These six questions all have a </span><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">Conclusion</strong><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);"> in the </span><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);">first sentence</strong><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">, </strong><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">which of course is not the most obvious place to find a conclusion. </span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-2"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">But </span><em class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">that\'s the point</em><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">! </span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">When we\'re doing </span><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">Main Conclusion</strong><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);"> and </span><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">Role</strong><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);"> questions, the test writers are intentionally trying to hide the conclusion, so that this otherwise-easy task can still be challenging.</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">The most common place to find the conclusion is after a Pivot, expressing some Rebuttal sentiment (65% of Main Conclusion questions).</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">The second most common place they\'ll stash it is in the first sentence (25% of Main Conclusion questions).</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">Only about 20% of the time on Main Conclusion does the paragraph end with the conclusion. That\'s why picking an answer that matches the final claim will usually be wrong (but not always!)</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">We want to practice reading Main Conclusion questions with a special ear for "upside-down" arguments, where we hear the conclusion and </span><em class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">then </em><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">hear the supporting ideas. </span></p></div></div></div></div><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pl-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><p class="ql-align-center"><strong class="ql-size-huge" style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);">Try these six questions,</strong></p><p class="ql-align-center"><span class="ql-size-large">focusing on how we\'d know that the 1st sentence is the conclusion.</span></p><p><br></p><p class="ql-align-center"><span style="color: rgb(183, 186, 189);">____________________________________________________________________</span></p><p><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">This exercise is about getting our brains used to the feel of a pattern. Focus on noticing how the first claim is an </span><strong class="ql-size-large">opinion</strong><span class="ql-size-large">, and then </span><strong class="ql-size-large">feeling </strong><span class="ql-size-large">how the subsequent claims go on to defend that initial opinion.</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-2"><span class="ql-size-large">Are there any </span><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);">Support Indicator</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> words that follow it? </span></p><p class="ql-indent-2"><span class="ql-size-large">(f.e. </span><strong class="ql-size-large">FABS</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> = for, after all, because, since) </span></p><p class="ql-indent-2"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-2"><span class="ql-size-large">Are there any </span><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);">Opinion Indicator</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> words in it? </span></p><p class="ql-indent-2"><span class="ql-size-large">(f.e. should, ought, probably, better) </span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">If we look at the claim in the first sentence and ask ourselves, "</span><strong class="ql-size-large">Why should we believe <em>that</em></strong><span class="ql-size-large">?", does the rest of an argument seem like an answer to that question? (it should)</span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div><div class="CalendarDraggableItem"><div draggable="true"><div class="schedule_item "><div class="schedule_item-inner"><div class="item_sub item_name" style="cursor: pointer;"><div class="item_image"><img src="https://assets.lsatlab.com/uploads/2021/08/Accuracy-Drill_LR.png" alt="Main Conclusion - Level 1"></div><div style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">Find the conclusion.</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">Make sure that it</span></p><ol><li class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">sounds like </span><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">Author\'s </span><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">Supported</strong><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);"> by at least one explicit claim.</span></li></ol><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><strong class="ql-size-huge" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">stimulus tendencies</strong></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">LSAC is seeking to make it harder than usual to find the Conclusion. Be aware that there will often be Intermediate Conclusions in these arguments that use obvious conclusion keywords. But the main conclusion usually isn\'t well-advertised like that. On this question type (and on Role), it\'s very rare to see the Conclusion be the final claim, prefaced by anything obvious like Therefore / Thus / So.</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">Instead, in more than 90% of Main Conclusion questions, </span><em class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">the Conclusion appears </em><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);"><em>earlier </em></strong><em class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">than (at least some of) the Support.</em></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">These are the two most common places they stash the conclusion:</span></p><ul><li class="ql-indent-1"><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">First sentence</strong></li><li class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">after a </span><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);">But / Yet / However</strong><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(52, 58, 64);"> pivot</span></li></ul></div></div></div></div><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pl-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><p class="ql-align-center"><strong class="ql-size-huge">Get 4 out of your last 5 correct,</strong></p><p class="ql-align-center"><span class="ql-size-huge">to pass this Level for </span><strong class="ql-size-huge" style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);">Main Conclusion</strong></p><p class="ql-align-center"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><strong class="ql-size-huge" style="color: rgb(87, 89, 98);">correct answer</strong></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">The correct answer just reproduces the meaning of the Conclusion. Sometimes it\'s a verbatim regurgitation. More commonly, they use synonyms or inverted syntax to present an equivalent meaning that still looks a little different.</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">f.e. if the conclusion appeared in the argument as "not all tornadoes should be avoided", then an equivalent claim would be "some tornadoes should not be avoided".</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">If you didn\'t already do the </span><strong class="ql-size-large">2-part Conclusion Check </strong><span class="ql-size-large">when you were first reading the argument and determining which claim is the conclusion, you can do it now (or again) --</span></p><ul><li class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">is this answer expressing an </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Opinion </strong><span class="ql-size-large">from our Author? (facts ≠ conclusions)</span></li><li class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">was this answer </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Supported</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> by at least one class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">When we\'re reading arguments in LR (which is about 80% of the time), our first job is to separate out the Main attached to Support, next-door to a Conclusion)</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><em class="ql-size-large">for, after all, because, since, and</em></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">Opinion indicators (opinions are usually Conclusions)</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><em class="ql-size-large">should, ought, obviously, clearly, apparently, evidently</em></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">Pivot indicators (usually attached to Rebuttal Conclusions)</span></p><p The argument opens with (or implies) some other point of view.</span></p><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">We typically see </span><strong class="ql-size-large">attribution </strong><span class="ql-size-large">language early on, such as:</span></p><ul><li><span class="ql-size-large">many people think that</span></li><li><span class="ql-size-large">some psychologists say that</span></li><li><span class="ql-size-large">it is commonly assumed that</span></li></ul><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">This is typically followed by a </span><strong class="ql-size-large">pivot</strong><span class="ql-size-large">: but, yet, however</span></p><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">Pivots represent a turning point in the argument from the background/counterpoint to the author\'s actual argument. From there we have to figure out which claim is the support, which is the conclusion.</span></p><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">We also want to articulate the rebuttal conclusion. For example, if we read, "Many people think the sun is predominantly iron. But they\'re wrong", we don\'t want to think of the Conclusion as "</span><em class="ql-size-large">They\'re wrong</em><span class="ql-size-large">". We want to articulate that the author\'s conclusion is saying, "the Sun is </span><strong class="ql-size-large">not </strong><span class="ql-size-large">predominantly iron."</span></p><p><br></p><p><br></p></div></div></div></div><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pl-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><p><span class="ql-size-large">Watch the video. la-trash"></i></div></div><div class="schedule_item-expand "><div class="row pb-4"><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pr-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><p class="ql-align-center"><span class="ql-size-huge">The Core Skill of RC</span></p><p class="ql-align-center"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">When learning scientists do research onto what techniques give students the most boost when it comes to retaining a passage, the clear champion is </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Self-Summarization</strong><span class="ql-size-large">.</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">This has way more benefit than annotating, note-taking, previewing the questions first, etc.</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">When we highlight or take notes, we often freeze our attention on specific words the passage used, but LSAT is testing us on the </span><em class="ql-size-large">meaning </em><span class="ql-size-large">of those words, not the words themselves.</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">When we self-summarize, we actually convert those words into meaning. We also make that meaning easier to remember by using conversational, gossipy language and by condensing things down to their core idea.</span></p></div></div></div></div><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pl-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><p class="ql-align-center"><span class="ql-size-huge">Fully-Baked Comprehension</span></p><p class="ql-align-center"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">Work on this skill of reading a paragraph of prose and then boiling it down to one core idea, stripping away academic language and putting it into plainspoken English, as though you\'re texting a one sentence summary of the paragraph to your friend.</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">It\'s almost impossible to reduce a whole paragraph into an effective, short synthesis without first understanding the purpose behind this paragraph. What does the author care most about you knowing, especially as it pertains to connecting to the next paragraph? </span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div><div class="CalendarDraggableItem"><div draggable="true"><div class="schedule_item  completed"><div class="schedule_item-inner"><div class="item_sub item_name" style="cursor: pointer;"><div class="item_image"><img src="https://assets.lsatlab.com/uploads/2021/08/Learn-A-Pattern_LR.png" alt="Rebuttal Conclusions"></div><div class="d-inline-flex flex-column ml-3"><h6 class="item_sub-text_dark mb-1">Rebuttal Conclusions</h6><p class="text-muted d-block mb-0">Patterns</p></div></div><div class="item_sub item_time">22 mins</div><div class="item_sub item_status" style="cursor: pointer;"><span class="m-badge m-badge--success m-badge--wide">Completed</span></div><div class="item_sub item_actions"><button class="btn l-btn-label-primary btn-sm">Info</button><a href="/practice-set-attempts/303599?scheduleactivityid=13250136&amp;userid=306842" class="btn l-btn-label-primary btn-sm ml-2">See Results</a><button class="btn l-btn-label-primary btn-sm ml-2">Takeaways</button></div><div class="item_sub item_type">Patterns</div><div class="item_sub item_arrow"><i class="la la-angle-down"></i></div><div class="item_sub item_delete"><i class="la la-trash"></i></div></div><div class="schedule_item-expand "><div class="row pb-4"><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pr-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><p><span class="ql-size-large">When we do </span><strong class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);">Main Conclusion </strong><span class="ql-size-large">questions, we expect LSAT to avoid putting the conclusion in its most obvious place (the final claim). We also expect them to avoid using obvious conclusion indicators (like therefore, thus, hence, so). </span></p><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">Instead, we expect the conclusion to usually either be the </span><strong class="ql-size-large">first claim</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> or be some </span><strong class="ql-size-large">rebuttal</strong><span class="ql-size-large">, typically introduced with Pivot words like but, however, yet. </span></p><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">Rebuttal conclusions usually have some sort of pronoun or referential language -- e.g. "But </span><em class="ql-size-large">this plan </em><span class="ql-size-large">would be likely to fail", "However </span><em class="ql-size-large">her conclusion</em><span class="ql-size-large"> is misguided". We need to replace those pronouns / referential ideas in a conclusion with the actual ideas they map back to.</span></p></div></div></div></div><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pl-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><p><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-huge">Try these four </span><strong class="ql-size-huge" style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);">Main Conclusion</strong><span class="ql-size-huge"> questions, all of which involve arguments with rebuttal conclusions.</span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div><div class="CalendarDraggableItem"><div draggable="true"><div class="schedule_item "><div class="schedule_item-inner"><div class="item_sub item_name" style="cursor: pointer;"><div class="item_image"><img src="https://assets.lsatlab.com/uploads/2026/01/Rebuttal-Rephrase.png" alt="Rebuttal Rephrase"></div><div class="d-inline-flex flex-column ml-3"><h6 class="item_sub-text_dark mb-1">Rebuttal Rephrase</h6><p class="text-muted d-block mb-0">AI Skills Training</p></div></div><div class="item_sub item_time">10 mins</div><div class="item_sub item_status" style="cursor: pointer;"></div><div class="item_sub item_actions"><button class="btn l-btn-label-primary btn-sm">Info</button><a href="/skills-training/8?scheduleactivityid=13250137&amp;studyactivityid=911" class="btn l-btn-label-primary btn-sm ml-2">Start</a><button class="btn l-btn-label-primary btn-sm ml-2">Finish</button></div><div class="item_sub item_type">AI Skills Training</div><div class="item_sub item_arrow"><i class="la la-angle-down"></i></div><div class="item_sub item_delete"><i class="la la-trash"></i></div></div><div class="schedule_item-expand "><div class="row pb-4"><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pr-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><p class="ql-align-center"><span class="ql-size-huge" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Articulate the Rebuttal Conclusion</span></p><p class="ql-align-center"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">This is one of our nerdiest phrases. It sounds complicated, but it\'s a very easy idea. We\'re essentially just flipping the logical light switch on an idea. </span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">EXAMPLE:</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Some people say that Lebron is the best basketball player ever. But they\'re wrong. After all, [evidence].</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">The conclusion is the sentence that says "They\'re wrong". But by itself it has no meaning. So we need to better articulate what the author means by rebutting "they\'re wrong".</span></p><p><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">BAD: They\'re wrong.</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">BETTER: People are wrong to say that Lebron is the best basketball player ever.</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">BEST: Lebron isn\'t the best basketball player ever.</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">We took the original attributed idea, "Lebron is the best", and just flipped its logical light switch to get "Lebron isn\'t the best".</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">This drill is about practicing that skill. </span></p></div></div></div></div><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pl-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><p class="ql-align-center"><span class="ql-size-huge">Practice This Skill for 7 Minutes</span></p><p class="ql-align-center"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">You\'ll be given an argument that contains a rebuttal conclusion. Your job is to express what that conclusion means in specific wording. If the conclusion is using any sort of pronoun / referential wording (e.g. "</span><strong class="ql-size-large">This </strong><span class="ql-size-large">reasoning is misguided / </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Such </strong><span class="ql-size-large">actions will not produce </span><strong class="ql-size-large">the intended effect</strong><span class="ql-size-large">"), you\'ll need to import the specific wording into those referential words/phrases. And of course you\'ll need to flip the logical light switch on the idea.</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">Flipping the switch on the idea is essentially the same idea as negating an answer choice (as we do in Necessary Assumption), or negating conclusions when we\'re trying to argue the Anti-Conclusion perspective (as we do on Flaw, Weaken, and other question types). </span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">Negating a claim means the same as "the </span><em class="ql-size-large">minimum </em><span class="ql-size-large">way to contradict this claim". (it has nothing to do with </span><strong class="ql-size-large">illegal negations</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> in conditional logic)</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><ul><li class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">When the truth value of a claim hinges on its </span><em class="ql-size-large">Quantifier</em><span class="ql-size-large">, you negate that quantifier.</span></li></ul><p><br></p><ul><li class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">When the truth value hinges on the Telling Part </span><strong class="ql-size-large">not </strong><span class="ql-size-large">being true, you negate the "not" by removing it.</span></li></ul><p><br></p><ul><li class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">If it\'s a conditional claim, the truth value hinges on its certainty. It\'s saying something is Always true or true in All cases. So you negate the certainty / the universal / the guarantee. By claiming "it\'s not certain", we are claiming that "there is at least one counterexample" or "it\'s possible for the trigger to be true but the outcome to be false". </span></li></ul><p><br></p><ul><li class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">For all other sentences, the truth value hinges on the verb, because the verb is what starts the Telling Part of the sentence. </span></li></ul></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div><div class="CalendarDraggableItem"><div draggable="true"><div class="schedule_item "><div class="schedule_item-inner"><div class="item_sub item_name" style="cursor: pointer;"><div class="item_image"><img src="https://assets.lsatlab.com/uploads/2021/08/Accuracy-Drill_LR.png" alt="Rebuttals Level 1"></div><div class="d-inline-flex flex-column ml-3"><h6 class="item_sub-text_dark mb-1">Rebuttals Level 1</h6><p class="text-muted d-block mb-0">Level Drill</p></div></div><div class="item_sub item_time">30 mins</div><div class="item_sub item_status" style="cursor: pointer;"></div><div class="item_sub item_actions"><button class="btn l-btn-label-primary btn-sm">Info</button><a href="/practice?type=LR&amp;questionsubtypes=Rebuttals&amp;difficulty=1&amp;tests=A%2CF1997%2C1%2C2%2C3%2C4%2C5%2C6%2C7%2C8%2C9%2C10%2C11%2C12%2C13%2C14%2C15%2C16%2C17%2C18%2C21%2C23%2C101%2C102%2C103%2C104%2C105%2C106%2C107%2C108%2C109%2C110%2C111%2C112%2C113%2C114%2C115%2C116%2C117%2C118%2C119%2C120%2C121%2C122%2C123%2C124%2C125%2C126%2C127%2C128%2C129%2C130%2C131%2C132%2C133%2C134%2C135%2C136%2C137%2C138%2C139%2C140%2C141%2C142%2C143%2C144%2C145%2C146%2C147%2C148%2C149%2C150%2C151%2C152%2C153%2C154%2C155%2C156%2C157%2C158%2C159&amp;showall=true&amp;studyactivityid=827&amp;scheduleactivityid=13250138&amp;milestoneid=85&amp;returnurl=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.lsatlab.com%2Fstudy-plan" class="btn l-btn-label-primary btn-sm ml-2">Start</a></div><div class="item_sub item_type">Level Drill</div><div class="item_sub item_arrow"><i class="la la-angle-down"></i></div><div class="item_sub item_delete"><i class="la la-trash"></i></div></div><div class="schedule_item-expand "><div class="row pb-4"><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pr-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><p><span class="ql-size-large">Over 10% of questions in an LR section feature </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Rebuttals</strong><span class="ql-size-large">.&nbsp;</span></p><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">When we see a Rebuttal within a </span><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);">1-speaker stimulus</span><span class="ql-size-large">, usually that stimulus will have this structure:</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">1)&nbsp;An </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Attributed</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> Claim/Argument </span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">(signified by wording like “Some people say / It is often assumed that / Many biologists think”)&nbsp;</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">2) A </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Pivot</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> </span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">(such as “but / yet / however”)</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">3) A </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Disagreement</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> (make sure to differentiate between harsh rebuttals like “This claim is false” and softer rebuttals like “This reasoning is faulty”. Many times authors are saying that the current evidence doesn’t prove the conclusion, but they’re not actually claiming that the conclusion is a false claim.)</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">4) The </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Author’s Evidence</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> (they’re often showing that a strong claim is false by pointing to a putative counterexample, or they’re showing that a hypothesis is unproven by pointing to a potential alternate explanation for the opposing evidence).&nbsp;</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">The other common variation is for the Author\'s Disagreement to have the opposing position embedded. For example, an argument might start this way:</span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><span class="ql-size-large">Crime is down 20% this year. However, it would be a mistake to credit this change to more aggressive policing. After all, ... </span></p><p class="ql-indent-1"><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">We can see in that 2nd sentence that the opposing position is, "Crime is down because of more aggressive policing."</span></p><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">In either case, the most important step in most questions involving rebuttals is to </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Articulate the Rebuttal Conclusion</strong><span class="ql-size-large">. </span></p><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">In the previous example that would mean saying to ourselves, "The author is concluding that </span><em class="ql-size-large">Crime is </em><strong class="ql-size-large"><em>not</em></strong><em class="ql-size-large"> down because of aggressive policing</em><span class="ql-size-large">." </span></p><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">When a Rebuttal involves a </span><span class="ql-size-large" style="color: rgb(7, 104, 162);">2-speaker stimulus</span><span class="ql-size-large">, usually the second person will be undermining the first person’s reasoning by pointing to an </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Alternate Explanation</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> for their evidence,&nbsp;by pointing to a </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Distinction </strong><span class="ql-size-large">or </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Counterexample</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> that goes against what the author was saying, or by showing that the first person\'s claim or plan has </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Faulty Implications</strong><span class="ql-size-large">. </span></p></div></div></div></div><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pl-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><h2 class="ql-align-center"><strong>Get 4 out of 5 correct </strong></h2><h2 class="ql-align-center">to pass this level.</h2><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">In </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Main Conclusion </strong><span class="ql-size-large">and </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Role </strong><span class="ql-size-large">questions, most conclusions are found </span><em class="ql-size-large">earlier </em><span class="ql-size-large">than the supporting ideas. About 60% of conclusions on Main Conclusion are some sort of Rebuttal claim.</span></p><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">On </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Method</strong><span class="ql-size-large">, there are four common forms of rebuttal:</span></p><ul><li><span class="ql-size-large">suggest the first person is making a dubious assumption</span></li><li><span class="ql-size-large">point out faulty implications / consequences of their claim or plan</span></li><li><span class="ql-size-large">suggest an alternate explanation for their evidence</span></li><li><span class="ql-size-large">point out a distinction or counterexample</span></li></ul><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">On </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Flaw</strong><span class="ql-size-large">, two of the 10 famous flaws relate to rebuttals:</span></p><ul><li><em class="ql-size-large">Ad Hominem</em><span class="ql-size-large">:&nbsp;&nbsp;the author dismisses a view because the source is biased or has some hypocritical/conflicting behavior or beliefs.</span></li><li><em class="ql-size-large">Unproven vs. Proven False</em><span class="ql-size-large">:&nbsp;&nbsp;the author cites someone\'s failure to prove X (either because they lack evidence or because they made a faulty argument in favor of X) and then concludes that X is false.</span></li></ul><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">On </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Fill in the Blank</strong><span class="ql-size-large">, if we see a rebuttal structure, the correct answer will usually sound like a Rebuttal conclusion, but trap answers will try to entice us into a too-strong version of that conclusion.</span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div><div class="CalendarDraggableItem"><div draggable="true"><div class="schedule_item "><div class="schedule_item-inner"><div </strong><span class="ql-size-large">questions, most conclusions are found </span><em class="ql-size-large">earlier </em><span class="ql-size-large">than the supporting ideas. About 60% of conclusions on Main Conclusion are some sort of Rebuttal claim.</span></p><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">On </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Method</strong><span class="ql-size-large">, there are four common forms of rebuttal:</span></p><ul><li><span class="ql-size-large">suggest the first person is making a dubious assumption</span></li><li><span class="ql-size-large">point out faulty implications / consequences of their claim or plan</span></li><li><span class="ql-size-large">suggest an alternate explanation for their evidence</span></li><li><span class="ql-size-large">point out a distinction or counterexample</span></li></ul><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">On </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Flaw</strong><span class="ql-size-large">, two of the 10 famous flaws relate to rebuttals:</span></p><ul><li><em class="ql-size-large">Ad Hominem</em><span class="ql-size-large">:&nbsp;&nbsp;the author dismisses a view because the source is biased or has some hypocritical/conflicting behavior or beliefs.</span></li><li><em class="ql-size-large">Unproven vs. Proven False</em><span class="ql-size-large">:&nbsp;&nbsp;the author cites someone\'s failure to prove X (either because they lack evidence or because they made a faulty argument in favor of X) and then concludes that X is false.</span></li></ul><p><br></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">On </span><strong class="ql-size-large">Fill in the Blank</strong><span class="ql-size-large">, if we see a rebuttal structure, the correct answer will usually sound like a Rebuttal conclusion, but trap answers will try to entice us into a too-strong version of that conclusion.</span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div><div class="CalendarDraggableItem"><div draggable="true"><div class="schedule_item  completed"><div </span></p><p><em>Strengthen, Weaken, Flaw, Evaluate, Nec/Suff assumption, Principle-Strengthen</em></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">read arguments and analyze their logical gaps / think about potential objections.</span></p><p><br></p><p><strong class="ql-size-large">Match Family</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> </span></p><p><em>Main Conclusion, Role, Method, Parallel, Parallel Flaw, other.</span></p><p><br></p><p><strong class="ql-size-large">Inference Family</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> </span></p><p><em>must be true, must be false, most supported, agree/disagree</em></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">read statements and pick the answer that is most supportably derived from those statements.</span></p><p><br></p><p><strong class="ql-size-large">Paradox</strong><span class="ql-size-large"> </span></p><p><span class="ql-size-large">These questions don\'t belong in the first two families, because we aren\'t reading arguments. But they don\'t belong in the last family, because we aren\'t picking the idea that is most derivable/provable from the statements. Instead, we\'re being offered new ideas, and the question is saying, "which of these does the most to resolve the confusing tension between the statements in the paragraph?"</span></p></div></div></div></div><div class="col-md-6"><div class="p-4 pl-md-3"><div class="ql-container ql-snow border-0"><div class="ql-editor"><p><br></p><p
